Was the firing squad really inept?

If ten of my weediest readers, with no prior training in musketry, tied me up, took aim, and fired for multiple rounds at close range, I would not expect to survive. If I did survive, I would be pretty perplexed, and infer that—miraculously—they were somehow okay with my blog posts.

Still, it would be all the more perplexing if my executioners did have training. The better shot I thought you all were in advance, the more perplexed I would be about surviving; conversely, the less training I thought you’d had, the less perplexed I’d have reason to be.

So here it makes sense to ask: is there any reason to think that the shooters were just terrible shots? (Bracketing, of course, the fact that they did miss, since a fair estimation of the prior probability that they’d collectively accidentally miss can’t include the fact that they did all miss in the background.)

For a giddy, glorious moment in my research, I thought the answer was ‘yes’. In Immortal: A Military History of Iran and Its Armed Forces, military historian Steven Ward describes the state of the Persian military in the Qajar period. The chapter is titled “Laughingstock”, which pretty much sums up the case. This bit, in particular, stuck out to me:61

The infantry was the most important branch in the standing army but was poorly motivated and trained. […] Garrison and regimental commanders, when called into action, would bring their units up to strength by the simple expedient of spending more money to recruit new men, put them into a uniform, and give them each a firearm. The hastily added soldiers were not significantly less skilled than their longer-serving comrades. Training was restricted to the most basic parade ground maneuvers and the perfunctory use of arms. Little or no time was devoted to musketry training on a firing range.

Further reading bore out this picture, at least in broad strokes. In an anonymous 1823 travelogue, a Russian observer witnessed Persian artillery manoeuvres. He noted that “out of more than one hundred shots, not a single one hit the target, though all of them landed quite close to it.”62 He also described a drill of artillery practice he observed in Tabriz as “a satire on our infantry” and wrote that “in general, the Persian sarbaz [soldier], or the so called regular army, are in their infancy.”63

However, our sources do not tell us that the firing squad was comprised of a random sample of the Persian military. They were, rather, members of the Behaduran regiment, which changes everything.

Behaduran soldiers were Russian-trained eastern European renegades who’d deserted the Russian army for the Persian one. The reason their involvement matters is that the Behaduran regiment was unusually well-trained and were, consequently, relied on for the most important jobs: according to one Russian chronicler, “it formed palace guards during the time of Fath ‘Ali Shah and his successor, Muhammad [Shah]. [The battalion] guarded the tranquility of the Persian rulers; it was their hope during attacks and in military campaigns.”64 According to Stephanie Cronin—the leading authority on the Behaduran regiment—“…sources agree that they constituted by far the best trained, most disciplined and most effective fighting force in the nizam-i jadid”65. And historian Goordaz Rashtiani concurs that they were “…one of the most disciplined and effective units of the Iranian army.”66

There is always the possibility that, by 1850, the Behaduran soldiers were not as sharp as they used to be, or that they were having a bad day, or whatever. And there is, of course, the fact that this was probably the first public firing squad executions in the history of the city, meaning the soldiers were unlikely to have done one before.

But of all the units in the Persian armed forces in 1850, the Behaduran was plausibly the least likely to fudge a clear shot at an immobile, adult-sized human target out of bumbling incompetence. Again, in my opinion, the accidental miss hypothesis is on the ropes.

Are there any comparable cases?

Before I trundle on to the two explanations I have more truck with (the conspiracy hypothesis and the miracle hypothesis), it’s worth asking whether we have any firing squad cases relevantly like this one. The short answer is that, as far as I can find, only a few cases come a little bit close.

One is the famous Washington bullet-hole story. On July 18, 1755, nine days after the Battle of Monongahela, George Washington wrote in a letter to his brother that “I had 4 Bullets through my Coat, and two Horses shot under me; yet escaped unhurt”, a claim he repeated in a letter to his mother. (There is a Christian book called Miracles in American History that lists the Washington bullet-hole story as one of them. However, the Amazon description said, and I quote, “YOU will be inspired as you uncover “Miracles in American History - 32 Amazing Stories of Answered Prayer.” ARE you aware of these past crises when America's fate hung in the balance?”, so I took a rain check on reading it.)

Narrowing our scope to firing squads, there are, according to certain military histories of World War One, heart-breaking cases where firing squads ordered to execute their targets couldn’t go through with it and missed. One account, quoted in Executed at Dawn: British Firing Squads on the Western Front 1914-1918, reads as follows67:

Early on the morning of 5 September, a small patrol of soldiers from Jimmy’s own unit entered a barn at Kemmel Château in Belgium to clean their weapons prior to re-engagement with the enemy. They were told that, first, they had a special duty to perform, and they were taken outside into a courtyard where they found their friend, Jimmy Smith, blindfolded and tied to an execution chair in front of a wall, with a white target pinned to his tunic, just above his heart. Protesting furiously to the commanding officer, the 12-man firing squad – 11 privates and a non-commissioned officer – was summarily ordered to execute Jimmy. The lads aimed and fired, the majority deliberately missing the target. However, Jimmy was wounded, the chair was knocked over and he lay writhing in agony on the ground.

The young officer in charge of the firing squad was shaking like a leaf, but he knew now that he had to finish Jimmy off by putting a bullet through his brain with his Webley pistol. He lost his nerve, however, and could not fire the the pistol in his hand as Jimmy continued to writhe in agony on the ground.

One of Jimmy’s friends, 23643 Private Richard Blundell, who hailed from Everton in Liverpool, was then ordered by the commanding officer to take the Webley pistol and kill Jimmy. Jimmy’s death was recorded on that day at 5.51 am.

There are also some cases where a bunch of people were lined up to be executed by firing squad, and then one of them survived by falling down and hiding among the dead bodies. For example, there is Serge Ross, a Jew in occupied France during World War II:

German soldiers surrounded the sawmill Serge worked in. The manager was ordered to pick 80 workers. Serge was one of them. They were lined up against a brick wall behind the village hall. German soldiers trained machine guns on the men. “I am going to die,” Serge thought. Just before the firing started, the man on his right, whom he barely knew, whispered, “Maybe I can save you.” He stepped in front and fell on top of Serge, shielding him from the gunfire. After the machine guns stopped, a German officer came through shooting survivors, but didn’t notice Serge was still alive.

If you google “people who survived firing squads”, the top result will be Wenceslao Moguel, a Mexican Handyman who survived a firing squad in 1915. However, Moguel’s survival is more of a medical miracle, since the bullets hit him in the body and face. (This is him after the shooting.)

Funnily enough, I stumbled across a firing squad miracle attributed to Padre Pio of all people. In Padre Pio: The Priest Who Bears the Wounds of Christ, Oscar De Liso writes of “…a seventeen-year-old girl, a spiritual daughter of Padre Pio’s, who believed that he had interceded with the Lord to save her life”:

During the war, she had been accused of Fascist crimes and had been caught one day by a group of Antifascists. Taking her to a spot in the open fields, they had stood her against a boulder and then moved away from her to assume the traditional position of the firing-squad. But before they could fire, a military column appeared, and the girl ran away. There were many soldiers in the column. For ninety-six hours, the troops were passing through San Giovanni Rotondo. While there were soldiers in and around the town, the Antifascists dared not show themselves. By the time they could leave their homes again, they had discovered that they had caught the wrong girl.68

But short answer: no. I haven’t yet found any properly comparable cases; nor have I found any comparable cases in an overtly religious context in which the survival is so providential-seeming that an inference to the miraculous suggests itself.

Did the firing squad fudge it on purpose?

In Resurrection and Renewal, Abbas Amanat spends a single sentence speculating about why the firing squad missed: “Possibly the unwilling troops missed their target deliberately”.69

If the firing squad missed on purpose, the miss was almost certainly coordinated. (Each soldier deciding to miss on purpose independently is no less a coincidence than each solider accidentally missing independently.)

And the person best positioned to coordinate a firing squad is its commander, which Nabil and Za‘ímu’d-Dawlih both identify as Sam Khan.

  1. The Christian Conscience Theory

Sam Kahn’s birth name was Samson Yakovlevich Makintsev. He was a Ukrainian-born soldier who had joined the Russian Dragoon regiment in 1799. For unknown reasons—rumour had it he’d stolen silver mouthpieces from the Russians’ trumpets—he deserted the regiment and joined the Persian military.

At the call of Abbas Mirza, the military-modernizing Crown Prince, Makintsev began recruiting Russians to the Persian army; as the deserters grew in number, they voiced complaints about their regiment’s Persian leadership. Mirza responded by forming a separate Russian unit under Makintsev.

Fast forward to 1826. According to historian Stephanie Cronin, “…by the time of the outbreak of a second war with Russia, in 1826, the deserters had developed qualms, and Makintsev tried to avoid taking a direct part in the fighting, declaring that the Russians had sworn on the Holy Gospel that they would not fire on fellow Christians.”70 Indeed, not only did Makintsev say that his men had sworn on the Holy Gospel that they wouldn’t fire on fellow Christians; according to a Russian biographical article published in 1876, Makintsev said “We swore on the Holy Gospel that we would not shoot at our co-religionists and we will not change our oath”71, implying, on a plain reading, that Khan agreed with the decision and the reason it was made.

Though we might question how pious Sam Kahn actually was (he murdered his first wife for adultery), his faith clearly meant a good deal to him. It is said in one Russian source that “despite a long stay among Muslims, Samson-khan preserved a fervent feeling of love for the native faith and that, for the manifestation of this feeling, he sacrificed his property and even risked incurring the indignation of the Persian government by constructing in one of his Azerbaijani villages a Christian temple…”.)72 It goes on the cite several pieces of anecdotal evidence to support the claim that Khan was a Christian throughout his life, including a long conversation between Khan and Captain Albrand, a Russian official, where the latter successfully appealed to Khan’s “deep religious conviction”73 to convince him to let 597 of his men return to Russia, crippling the strength of his regiment74. It also notes that Khan “…rarely went a day without setting aside time to read the Gospel and the Psalms.”75

So, then, here is something we can plug into out background knowledge when approaching the martyrdom of the Bab: Sam Khan—a zealous Christian in a Shi’i country—is known to have defied the Persian state once before and refused, alongside his men, to fire on Russian soldiers for reasons of religious conscience. He is also, in another episode, known to have surrendered a large portion of his troops to Russia, allegedly for reasons of religious conscience. What little we know of Khan’s psychology suggests that he was someone whose religious conscience affected him, to the point of prompting sometimes costly decisions on his part.

Now fast forward to the hour before the Báb’s execution. According to Nabil’s Narrative, Makintsev (referred to by Nabil as ‘Sam Kahn’) felt uneasy about firing on the Bab, for reasons of religious conscience. According to Nabil, Makintsev was, prior to execution,

“…finding himself increasingly affected by the behaviour of his Captive and the treatment that had been meted out to him. He was seized with great fear lest his action should bring upon him the wrath of God. “I profess the Christian Faith,” he explained to the Báb, “and entertain no ill-will against you. If your Cause be the Cause of the Truth, enable me to free myself from the obligation to shed your blood.” “Follow your instructions”, the Báb replied, “and if your intention be sincere, the Almighty is surely able to relieve you from your perplexity.””76

Drawing it all together: one possible conspiracy theory is that the firing squad was secretly ordered to miss (perhaps by aiming—all together—up at the ropes), high above the Báb and his disciple, in an effort to create the impression of a spectacular miracle that would get them off the hook for the Báb’s execution. And one speculative motive might be that Makinstev was having qualms of religious conscience, as Nabil’s Narrative suggests.

This is a fun theory and might be true. Nevertheless, on the merits, I think it suffers from at least eight drawbacks:

  1. First, the Christian firing squad was hand-picked to carry out the execution precisely because the government thought they were the least likely regiment to flake. Presumably, Persian officials living at the time would’ve had a much keener sense of the prior probability that each regiment would flake or mess up, and chose the Makintsev’s regiment precisely on that basis.77 Remember: the Báb’s execution was a high-stakes public display, aimed at humiliating the Bábis and crushing their spirits; from the perspective of the government, it could not be allowed to fail.

  2. Second, the hypothesis takes a hit from the fact that—according to Siphir, Gobineau, Sharif, Blunt, Azal, Browne, Za‘ímu’d-Dawlih, and the guy that Tweedy interiviews—the Báb’s disciple, Mírzá Muḥammad-’Alí, was shot by firing squad #1. This claim is contradicted by Kazem-Bek, ʻAbdu’l-Bahá, and Zarandi, who say Muḥammad-’Alí survived the first volley alongside the Báb, and by the Nuqṭat al-Kāf, which says Muḥammad-’Alí was tied up and shot before the Báb, falling at his master’s feet. On balance, the majority view is most likely, both because it’s the majority view and because Muḥammad-’Alí’s miraculous survival would make sense as a religious embellishment. The reason the conspiracy hypothesis takes a hit from this detail is that, by several accounts, Muḥammad-’Alí was positioned very close to the Báb. Nuqtat al-Kaf narrates that “[t]hey first tied up Jináb-i-Ákhúnd Mullá Muḥammad-i-‘Alí at the place at which he would be shot by the firing squad behind the Báb. He begged, ‘Permit me to be bound in such a way that my head may rest on the breast of my Beloved.’ They granted his request.” Gobineau says the condemned were “suspended side by side”. Supplying more detail, ‘Abdu’l-Baha narrates that “[a]n iron nail was hammered into the middle of the staircase of the very cell wherein they were imprisoned, and two ropes were hung down. By one rope the Báb was suspended and by the other rope Áqá Muḥammad-‘Alí, both being firmly bound in such wise that the head of that young man was on the Báb’s breast.” Zarandi says, similarly, that “Sám K͟hán ordered his men to drive a nail into the pillar that lay between the door of the room that Siyyid Ḥusayn occupied and the entrance to the adjoining one, and to make fast two ropes to that nail, from which the Báb and His companion were to be separately suspended. Mírzá Muḥammad-’Alí begged Sám K͟hán to be placed in such a manner that his own body would shield that of the Báb. He was eventually suspended in such a position that his head reposed on the breast of his Master.” (The detail about where Muḥammad-’Alí’s head was positioned fits nicely with Za‘ímu’d-Dawlih’s assertion that he “asked for his face to be placed at the Báb’s feet, but this request was not accepted.”) Subh-i-Azal, Baha’u’llah’s estranged half-brother, also notes briefly that “they [the soldiers] bound him [Muḥammad-’Alí], together with His Holiness the Point, and the soldiers discharged their muskets.” So it looks like the Báb and his disciple were suspended with their bodies together; but, in that case, given that 19th century muskets weren’t extremely accurate (even if they were accurate enough to kill someone at close range if multiple muskets were being used), then this feature of the story strains against any version of the collective miss hypothesis, since now, it seems, the bullets weren’t all being aimed way up at the ropes (or to off to the side, or whatever), but in the direction of the condemned.

  3. Third, as much as I tried to dress up the case for this theory going in, it is not as well-motivated as I made out. Kahn’s extensive military career shows that he was not averse to firing on Muslims who were co-religionists only in the broad sense of being Children of Abraham. All we get from the 1826 incident, is that at most he was averse, at that point in time, to firing on Orthodox Christians; and from the perspective of a Christian foreigner, the Bábis—who were, in a sense, a sect of a sect of a sect of Islam—were surely not co-religionists from Kahn’s perspective.

  4. Fourth, in a similar vein, we don’t know whether Khan was voicing his own pangs of conscience in 1826, voicing the scruples of his men on their behalf as their commander, or giving a high-minded, pious excuse for avoiding battle with a dangerous Russian army, comprised of their compatriots and former comrades. So although the 1826 incident superficially rhymes with the incident of the Báb’s execution, I don’t think it substantially hikes up the prior probability of a Christian commander risking his own safety by telling his men (each a potential whistle-blower with a higher loyalty to the Shah and his government) to collectively miss their target in order to get of the hook for killing who he could only have regarded as a false prophet.

  5. Fifth, like all conspiracy theories, its probability wanes as the number of conspirators waxes. If I’m right that the firing squad was massive, the ex ante risk of covertly ordering his troops to humiliate the Persian government by staging a miracle in front of a large crowd would have been substantial, since the more soldiers Makintsev had to order, explicitly, to miss, the higher the risk that one of them would say something to the wrong person and get everyone else—including Makintsev—into hot water. (This point has to be qualified somewhat: according to Behrze’s biography, Khan had a good deal of influence over Hamza Mirza, who supervised the execution of the Báb.78 If so, this may have lessened the degree to which Khan conspiring to stage a miracle would have been life-threatening, since maybe he could’ve counted on Mirza for protection.)

  6. Sixth, to the extent that the theory relies on the dialogue in Nabil’s Narrative being historical, the baby comes along with the bathwater—the very scene in which Makintsev expresses his qualms ends with the Bab verbally telling him to do his duty. It would be a bit odd if Makintsev’s part of the dialogue was historical but that Bab’s part of the dialogue was completely invented. More generally, Nabil’s Narrative contains a lot of episodes that sceptics would do well to be wary of, like the Bab being discovered in conversation with his amanuensis with an “expression of undisturbed serenity”79, or that “[t]he very moment the shots were fired, a gale of exceptional severity arose and swept over the whole city. A whirlwind of dust of incredible density obscured the light of the sun and blinded the eyes of the people. The entire city remained enveloped in that darkness from noon till night.”80 Given that, like these other details, Makintsev’s religious scruples go unmentioned in other sources, relying on Nabil for this otherwise unattested story—while ignoring him for all the others—is a tricksy needle to thread. (However, in fairness to Nabil’s Narrative, the fact that what little we know about Khan reveals him to have been a man who let his religious conscious get to him and affect his actions is independent evidence for the reliability of Nabil’s narration—at least on the martyrdom front.)

  7. Seventh, unless we think that Khan left his life-long orthodox faith to become a Babi right before the execution—which not even Nabil claims—it’s puzzling in the extreme why a pious Christian would, of all things, stage a counterfeit miracle on behalf of the prophet of a new, Islamicate sect.

  8. We know that just two years before the martyrdom, in 1848, a Babi merchant named Āqā ʿAlī Riżā was arrested by Sam Khan, “who flogged him on the pretext of blasphemy and extorted a large sum of money from him”81. If Khan had a Road to Damascus moment in 1950, he really had a Road to Damascus moment in 1850.

The New Muslim Theory

One fact I haven’t mentioned yet is that over the years, a large part of the Behaduran unit converted to Islam. Cronin writes that “[a]t first, the majority of both officers and men kept their Christian faith. Of those who decided to settle in Iran, about two-thirds eventually converted to Islam, apparently in order to avoid possible repatriation, and became popularly known as new Muslims (yeni Musulman).”82 Though most of the sources we’ve read that comment on the detachment’s religious make-up refer to it as ‘Christian’, Sharif writes of “the Bahadur regiment, composed of men who had formerly been Christians”.83

Let’s assume, then, that the detachment ordered to kill the Bab was partly Christian, but partly—maybe mostly—made up of Muslim converts. A different motive for our naturalistic conspiracy theory is that the men were worried about killing a descendant of the Prophet. Amanat writes that “[t]he choice of the Bahādurān was prudent since it was suspected that Muslim regiments might not volunteer to take the responsibility for the killing of a descendent of the Prophet. Sām Khān seems to have had some apprehension about carrying out the orders, but succumbed to Farrāshbāshī’s pressure.”84

What if the new Muslims were so scrupulous about killing a descendent of the Prophet that they pressured Khan to command everyone to miss? (Note: on the authority of Behrze’s biography of Khan, I proceed on the assumption that he himself remained a Christian. Abbas Amanat cites an early nineteenth century Muslim source claiming that Khan had converted to Islam; but until I get access to that history—I’m working on it—I’m deferring to Behrze’s biography.)

Aside from the general problems that plague every version of the conspiracy hypothesis, there are two specific problems attending this one. While two thirds of the regiment may have nominally ‘converted’ to Islam, we should be realistic about how sincere their conversions were likely to have been (and, correspondingly, whether it’s likely that they were by this stage so deep in Shi’i lore that they had theological scruples about killing a Descendent of the Prophet—even one who had abrogated the Qur’an.) As Cronin writes of the Behaduran converts, “[t]hey were […] completely uninterested in religious formalities and at Muslim religious services they continued their Orthodox ritual of repeatedly crossing themselves.”85

Second, the motivation is hard to make sense of. If the Muslim soldiers were scrupulous about getting their hands dirty, but fine with letting other people do the job afterwards (they would’ve foreseen, surely, that if they missed, other soldiers would be commanded to execute the Bab—which is what happened), why didn’t they petition Khan to have the Christian men take the shot, and leave the scrupulous converts out of it? And it seems a strange form of religious scrupulosity that would cause non-Babi Muslims to stage a counterfeit miracle the lent credibility to a heretical prophet who had abrogated Islamic law, just because that heretic was a descendent of the Prophet.

The Intimidation Theory

One more conspiracy hypothesis, for the road. According to Siphir, the court historian writing in 1858, the firing squad missed because they were scared of the Babis:

On Monday, 27 Sha’bán, on orders of Hamzih Mírzá, soldiers of the Bahádurán regiment, of Christian confession, were to shoot them. Since these soldiers had often heard about the disturbances caused by the followers of the Báb in the cities, being reluctant to execute the Báb, they aimed their guns high and low, as well as to the right and to the left of the Báb so that he was not hurt at all. However, this time Mullá Muḥammad-’Alí, his disciple, was killed. He was firmer than the Báb, for when he was wounded, he turned to the Báb and said: “Are you not satisfied with me?” In brief, at this moment an accidentally discharged bullet hit the rope with which the Báb’s arms were tied, and he was freed, and ran away, and hid in the room of one of the soldiers.86

This is the only conspiracy hypothesis outright endorsed by one of our sources (although, interestingly, Siphir supplements his conspiracy theory with an appeal to providence, claiming that God ensured that the men would miss so as to expose the Bab as a coward.)

In an old issue of World Order, a Baha’i periodical, the authors of an article on the Martyrdom of the Bab accuse Siphir’s story of incoherence:

In spite of these and other inaccuracies, Sipihr, like Sheil, confirms the fact that the first volley fired at the Báb did not hurt Him though it allegedly killed Mullá Muḥammad-'Alí. Beyond this point Sipihr's story becomes virtually incoherent. Thus, having stated that the first volley killed the Báb's faithful disciple, he, in the next sentence, says that Mullá Muḥammad-'Alí "was wounded." Wounded? Was he not killed by the volley? That same volley was supposedly fired by the soldiers who had purposely aimed their guns too high, too low, too far to the right, or too far to the left. How did they then manage to kill (or was it wound?) Mullá Muḥammad-'Alí and to cut the ropes "with which the Báb's arms were tied"? Yet even this garbled story agrees with the rest in the one most amazing particular of the Báb's martyrdom—the inefficacy of the first volley.87

I think they’re being a bit harsh. It’s possible Siphir is saying Muḥammad-’Alí was wounded and then died from those wounds, just in a wonky order. And while the fact that Muḥammad-’Alí was wounded and killed puts probabilistic pressure on the idea that the soldiers were intentionally missing, the claim is not strictly incoherent. Still, I take World Order’s point that Siphir’s account feels a bit garbled, at least compared to other accounts.

Is it credible that the Behaduran soldiers missed because they were, in some way, scared of the Babis? In terms of positive evidence, the only source we have that makes this claim is Siphir; since Siphir was writing at the pleasure of the Shah, we’d positively expect him to throw out a non-Babi explanation of the event regardless of whether it was well-evidenced. Indeed, you might even expect him to give an outwardly hostile explanation, regardless of whether it was true (and he does this, twice: when he appeals to Babi violence, and when appeals to God’s desire to vindicate Islam over the Babi heresy.) Given especially that Siphir does not allude to any evidence for this interpretation, his say-so doesn’t take us very far.

But is the idea plausible independently? Certainly it is hard to disprove; but at the same time, I’m not aware of any evidence in its favour (beyond the general fact that there had been some, mostly defensive, Babi violence in other cities in the years leading up to the Bab’s execution), and it strikes me as facially implausible: the Babis were a disempowered and harshly persecuted religious minority, and they were not heavily clustered in Tabriz. It’s unclear, therefore, what these professional soldiers had to fear from the Babis, who were largely clerics, landowners, government employees, merchants, artisans—things of that nature.(Conversely, it is clear that the Babis had a lot to fear from the government, given the brutal spate of Babi executions that followed the execution of the Bab.)88

The Disjunctive Conspiracy Theory

Of course, the conspiracy theorist need not maintain that any of the preceding conspiracy theories are, by themselves, more probable than the miracle hypothesis. All she needs to claim is that the disjunction of all the available conspiracy theories (the Christian Conscience Theory or the New Muslim Theory or the Intimidation Theory, etc.) is more probable than the disjunction of all the available miracle hypotheses. That choice I leave to the reader. Before I do, though, let’s consider some different aspects of the miracle hypothesis, starting with an objection to it.

The world’s first self-refuting vindicatory miracle?

Imagine a prophet called Bob who—in his capacity as prophet—proclaims that no miracle is ever evidence for any religion.

Now imagine Bob founds a religion (which this doctrine about miracles is part of) and gets martyred for it. Three days later, Bob comes back from the dead and zooms up into the sky.

Assuming Bob’s resurrection was genuinely supernatural, here is a specific miracle hypothesis that won’t fly: an omni-rational God agreed with all of Bob’s assertions, and wanted to evidence their truth with a miracle.

The reason this miracle hypothesis won’t fly is that one of Bob’s assertions was that no miracle is ever evidence for any religion, and so an omni-rational God could not have agreed with that teaching and then sought to provide evidence for all of Bob’s religious assertions by working a miracle (for, if God did that, he’d be simultaneously agreeing that no miracle is evidence for any religion whilst trying to evidence a religion with a miracle, which is irrational and double-minded.)

The most important living scholar of the Báb’s writings is Nader Saiedi. In an essay on the Báb’s worldview, Saiedi writes: “[o]ne of the central teachings of the Báb is that miracles, as the breaking of the laws of nature, have no relevance to the mission of the prophet—which is the spiritual and moral education of humanity. Therefore, miracles cannot function as legitimate evidence of truth.”

If the claim that “miracles cannot function as legitimate evidence of truth” is something the Báb claimed, then the miracle of the Báb can’t have been intended to vindicate all of his religious claims (at least, not if the miracle was divine).

Likewise, if the claim that “miracles cannot function as legitimate evidence of truth” was one of the Báb’s “central teachings”, then the miracle of the Báb can’t have been intended to vindicated all of his central teachings. (Possibly, it was meant to vindicate a subset of his central teachings; but then we should be correspondingly less confident in any particular central teaching, since now we’re not sure which ones God endorses and which He doesn’t.)

Of course, there are other theistic hypotheses we could go for, e.g.,

  • Before his death the Báb prayed for God to let him finish his conversation, and God obliged;

  • God wanted to testify to the Báb’s general holiness but not his teachings;

  • God didn’t want the Christians to get their hands dirty, so he let the Muslims get their hands dirty instead (this is something a Christian philosopher actually once suggested);

  • God wanted to expose the Báb as a coward and vindicate Islam;

  • Satan and his minions wanted to cast doubt on the miracle case for Catholicism by doing a miracle on behalf of the one of the most fruit-bearing religions in human history;

  • Etc.

But the hypothesis that the miracle was done to provide legitimate evidence for the Báb’s central teachings will be substantially hobbled.

Fortunately, this puzzle was quickly resolved. I shot Professor Saiedi an email asking for clarification on what he meant by “miracles cannot function as legitimate evidence of truth”. Graciously, he replied,

What I meant by not being “legitimate evidence” is that humans have no legitimate right to ask for miracles as the evidence of the truth of the Manifestations of God. If the Manifestation decides to work miracles that is a further and generous expression of his might and truth. But in terms of divine justice and the sufficiency of evidence, no miracle is needed. From a Baha’i perspective, most miracles attributed to sacred ones are either a fabrication by the believers or, if mentioned in scriptures, have symbolic meaning.

Pending further information about the Báb’s theology of miracles, I’m not aware of any reason to think the ‘vindicatory miracle’ hypothesis is self-defeating, as convenient as that would have been.

The miracle of the Bab is Hume-proof

In his famous and overrated essay “Of Miracles”, David Hume defines a miracle as “a transgression of a law of nature by a particular volition of the Deity, or by the imposition of some invisible agent.”

In a less famous and more justly-rated essay, “The Miraculous”, R. F. Holland gives an example that, to my mind, show’s Hume’s definition to be implausibly restrictive.89 Holland tells the story of a child who gets his toy car stuck on a railway crossing; as he busies himself with peddling loose, his mother screams in horror as a train speeds down the tracks. Suddenly, seconds before collision, the driver suffers the knock on effects of a heavy lunch and a fight with a colleague, and faints. The train stops just a few feet from the boy, sparing his life.

In this case, Holland thinks, it would make sense for the mother to call this insane stroke of luck a ‘miracle’ even after finding out the natural cause of the train stopping, given its providential timing.

If your intuition isn’t pumped by this example, just crank up the volume and imagine that fifty trains were all hurtling down fifty different tracks that all—because of ham-fisted railway design—converged right at where the child was peddling; if each driver, for outwardly probabilistically independent reasons, all fainted due to high blood pressure at just the right moment, this would clearly be in the running for ‘miracle’ status. (If you think a miracle must be religiously coded to count as one, throw in that the child was a religious prodigy who was in the process of founding a world religion.)

Some alleged miracles aren’t like Holland’s train miracle; the resurrection of Jesus, for example, would require a suspension of the laws of nature if it happened, as would St. Joseph of Cupertino’s levitations. However, other putative miracles are relevantly like the train miracle—e.g., the miracle of the Báb. If it was a bona fide miracle, the mechanism could have involved divine intervention (where God curves the bullets like Magneto) but it could equally have been providentially arranged, consistent with known laws of nature. Guns have been known to miss human targets, even if never on this scale.

Since Hume’s argument against believing miracle testimony only targets miracles of the former kind (the transgression-of-a-natural-law kind), it doesn’t directly bear on miracles of the latter, providential, kind. Some of Hume’s other points against believing miracle testimony still might apply (e.g., that it’s untrustworthy if it comes from “ignorant and barbarous nations”), but they are less ambitious and less interesting.

So, if you are everlastingly checked-out and think, for some ignoble Humean reason, that the prior probability of law-violating miracles is, always and everywhere, so prohibitively low that nearly nothing should convince you in the way of testimony that a law-violating miracle happened, you are still not off the hook for miracles like the Holland’s train miracle or the miracle of the Báb, which admit of a natural, ‘providential coincidence’ reading.

And, if you’ve been hoodwinked into thinking that the ‘transgression of a law of nature by a particular volition of the Deity’ is essential to the definition of a ‘miracle’, just coin a new, nearby concept, a ‘schmiracle’ or a ‘miracle*’, and give that a more expansive definition that includes wild, religiously conspicuous coincidences that cohere with the laws of physics like the schmiracle of the train or the miracle* of the Báb.

A coincidence miracle selection effect?

If an apparent miracle happens at a formative stage of a major religion, you might reasonably wonder if there’s a selection effect at play. Namely: religions that have odd, once-in-a-million coincidences at their early stages are more likely to become big and successful, precisely because the odd, once-in-a-million coincidence at their early stages contribute to the religion’s success.

Take Jesus’ resurrection. To account for the conversions of James and Paul, as well as the other alleged post-mortem experiences of the Risen Christ, some sceptics feel pressure to concede that Something Strange happened after Good Friday (e.g., a string of grief hallucinations). If the sceptic grants that Jesus’s tomb was found empty by two of his female followers, they’ll probably have to say Something Strange about that too (e.g., it was visited by grave robbers, or the tomb was misidentified, or whatever.)

The Christian, at this point, could reply as follows: “Ok, maybe, but isn’t it weird that this very unusual string of events happened in the context of a religious figure whose religion then went on to be the largest and most influential in human history?”

Sceptics, in response, can point out that the two things are probabilistically dependent: whatever explains why belief in the resurrection arose, the fact that it did arise is why the post-Easter Christian movement regained its confidence and started preaching the gospel to the world. Of course, you couldn’t predict the global success of Christianity merely from whatever weird, unusual series of events happened after the crucifixion; but those events have a lot to do with the subsequent success of Christendom, and so the sceptic isn’t saddled with as big a coincidence as our imagined Christian wants to make out.

Is a similar thing going on here? Is the success of the Baha’i Faith probabilistically dependent on the weird, once-in-a-million firing squad miracle, or are they completely independent of one another?

Historical events are unlike unmarked cards or fair coins, so it would be silly to say that the ‘miracle’ of the Báb is strictly probabilistically independent of the Baha’i Faith’s subsequent success. But from what I’ve read so far about the post-execution plight of the Babi movement—and the subsequent success of the Baha’i Faith—there’s no indication that the Miracle of the Báb had much of anything to do with the religion’s success.

Indeed, according to Amanat, “[t]he execution of the Bab deprived the movement of its charismatic leader. Firm action of the government, far more effective than the adversity of the ‘ulama, helped to reduce the Babis to a despised heresy. The new prophet’s human vulnerability turned the ephemeral sympathy of the miracle-seeking public into indifference and soon into hostility.”90

Certainly, the death of the Bab was useful in ginning up international sympathy for the Babi movement and the notoriety of the Bab’s teachings. But what is less clear is whether the alleged miracle was crucial to that. The Bab’s execution was, by itself, a major political event—the miracle was the cherry on top.

Subsequently, the Babi-Baha’i taboo on miracle apologetics prevented the martyrdom for being wheeled out as an evangelistic argument, and, consequently, you won’t find Baha’is using the Martyrdom as an apologetic rod with which to thump sceptics. As as result, my sense is that the martyrdom miracle is largely independent of the Baha’i Faith’s success, which, if true, undercuts the appeal to a coincidence miracle selection effect.

Conclusion

The Martyrdom of the Báb is baffling, and I don’t really know what to say about it.

The most plausible naturalistic explanation will have to be one that doesn’t render all the misses probabilistically independent, and the most plausible of those is a conspiracy theory: a collective, intentional miss. However, the intentional miss hypothesis is riddled with bullets it is forced to bite once the theory is fleshed out in detail—in particular, the theory posits that a group of soldiers who were specifically selected because they were anticipated to have no religious qualms about executing a man who would have been, from their perspective, the author of a sect of a sect of a sect of Islam, risked their own employment, safety, and possibly lives (a risk that increases with the size of the firing squad, which—I have argued—was massive) because they had some unlikely qualm about executing the Bab; and that—if we accept the early, multiple attestation for the claim that Muḥammad-’Alí was shot during the first volley, the hypothesis takes a further hit of disconfirmation, since Muḥammad-’Alí’s death is surprising on the hypothesis that the marksmen were all aiming up at the ropes and away from the condemned.

Faffing in the direction of ‘maybe their muskets/rifles weren’t the most accurate guns in the world’ or ‘the maybe marksmen weren’t the best marksmen in the world’ or ‘maybe the Báb fell down at just the right moment—when there was enough smoke to mask his fall but not enough bullets to render his death a certainty’—may ease the tension a little bit; but it is still, I fear, cope, and sceptics who try to thread this needle should concede as much.

In the overtly religious context of the miracle (the Báb was a major religious prophet who sowed the seeds of a growing global religion), the miracle hypothesis serves itself up on a silver platter—it is, after all, the literal bringing-to-life of a philosophical thought experiment that philosophers of religion have been using for decades as an allegory for divine design in the context of a new religion’s prophet who claimed divine authorisation for his teachings.

Nevertheless, whether you want to go in for some version of the miracle hypothesis will obviously depend on your theological priors (how likely religious miracles are in general, how likely they are in conspicuously religious contexts, how likely they are in this religious context, how likely they are to be faked by deceptive demons who want to discredit Catholic miracle apologetics on Substack, etc.); and that, dear reader, I leave to you.

Postscript

In writing this piece, I’ve been impressed by extent to which I am not a historian, and the extend to which analytic philosophy graduate students are no better equipped—by dint of their training—to do amateur history than anyone else is. Hopefully, by making the sources available, I have at least helped by putting the information in your hands, so you can investigate the truth for yourself, with greater ease, and not have to rely on what an analytic philosophy graduate student says the sources say, however confident they seem in their pronouncements.

Over the coming days and weeks, I expect and welcome corrections and new information (or new spins on old information that I overlooked). As ‘Abdu'l-Bahá says, “[t]he shining spark of truth cometh forth only after the clash of differing opinions”. Should corrections come in, I will, after fact-checking, try to keep a tab of them here.

Finally, if you are interested in keeping up with my private shower-thoughts about the Baha’i Faith, which I am researching in a personal capacity, check out my secret, sister Substack, Baha’i: An Independent Investigation.

item.title: “What is this? A dilemma for ants?”
item.description: I have a question about the protestant dilemma
item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
Two sibling ants, Anthony and Anthonia, are arguing on tail of an antelope. ‘I’m right, you’re wrong’, squeaks Anthony. ‘No, I’m right, you’re wrong’, cries Anthonia.

The dispute is simple. Anthony adheres to ‘My Mummyism’, according to which whatever Mummy says is correct. Anthonia believes in ‘Corroborationism’, according to which Mummy speaks truly only when corroborated by Papa.

Smirking, Anthony folds his legs. ‘Corroborationists can’t answer THIS dilemma—and they’re PANICKING’, he crows.

‘What dilemma?’, Anthonia asks, annoyed.

“Anthonia CAN’T SOLVE the Corroborationist Dilemma’, Anthony titters, getting a million hits on YouTube.

‘Dude, what dilemma?’

‘It’s simple. Remember that trip Mummy went on when she carried 27 crumbs of bread at once by herself? You believe that happened, right?’

‘I guess…’

‘Aha! Papa never corroborated that story! So therefore, according to you, it’s not correct, and so your belief about it is false. Thus the corroborationist dilemma: you can have your corroborationism or your cherished childhood belief that mummy carried 27 bread crumbs to the ant hill by herself—but you absolutely can’t have both.’

‘Hmmm. Shoot, I really thought Papa did corroborate that story…’

‘Nope! He didn’t. Corroborationism is cooked. Time to submit to Mummy. Ad maiorem Mummy gloriam! This video is sponsored by Claude.’

  1. Either the Catholic Church and her bishops aren’t reliable or else they are.

item.title: The Puzzle of Hell Solved?
item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
In “The Puzzle of Hell Solved”, economist, blogger, and Danny DeVito lookalike suggests an underrated solution to the problem of hell:

One problem for Christians is how to make the existence of Hell, eternal torture for sinners, consistent with the existence of a benevolent and all powerful God. A possible solution is to deny that Christian doctrine requires the existence of Hell. Observing an online argument over that question, one based on interpretations of the text of scripture, it occurred to me that there is a simpler solution to the problem of making scriptural references to Hell consistent with a benevolent God, a solution that should be obvious to an economist if not to a theologian.

The belief in Hell is useful as an incentive not to sin. Once a sinner has died, torturing him serves no useful purpose, so there is no reason for a benevolent God to go through with it. If it is still possible for the sinner to reform and be saved he should be given another chance, as portrayed by C.S. Lewis in The Great Divorce. If he is a hopeless case he can be painlessly removed from existence.

The obvious explanation of the available evidence, the explanation consistent with both the text and divine benevolence, is that scriptural references to Hell are a strategic lie. I do not know if there is evidence in scripture that God sometimes lies but I do not see how there could be evidence that he never does.

Unfortunately, Friedman’s gambit won’t work for the new spate of Catholic converts, who are, it seems, stuck with an absolutist deontological prohibition on lying. Since normative theories aspire to generality—they should apply to all moral agents who are relevantly alike—the magisterial prohibition likely extends to all asserters with a rational nature, divine and human both, meaning God cannot lie for consequentialist reasons conditional on Catholicism. (Of course, magisterial teaching on lying could itself be a lie. But at that point, I mean, what are we even doing with our lives.)

In friend-of-the-blog Joe Schmid’s 25-hour conversion video, part three, he discusses how he was able, over time, to overcome what initially seemed to be crushing philosophical objections to eternal hell. A core plank of one model he explores has it that the damned—that is, sinners in hell—enjoy net-positive lifetime wellbeing. The damned suffer punishment and the pain of loss, sure, but their ill-being is outweighed by greater wellbeing—pleasure, desire satisfaction, objective list goods, what have you.

Of course, as a really, really hopeful universalist, I’m going to think this is what infernalists should say, for the simple reason that it assimilates infernalism to universalism, which results in it being more plausible—a result universalism predicts.

The happiness-in-hell compromise has other advocates, including Alexander Pruss, ibn Arabi, and Martin Lembke. In 1892, the English Catholic convert George Mivart published an article in defence of the view that the damned enjoy ‘natural happiness’ in hell. As historian Simon Mayers recounts, “[t]he result was a torrent of letters, sermons and articles in various Catholic newspapers and periodicals, including the Tablet, the Month, the Irish Ecclesiastical Record, the Franciscan Annals and La Civiltà Cattolica. Some were sympathetic, though most were ambivalent or hostile.”

In 1893, Mivart’s writings on hell were placed on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum. Docile at first, Mivart protested the decision in 1899 and “published a series of articles that were critical of the Church”. In 1900, “Cardinal Archbishop Vaughan circulated a letter which excluded Mivart from receiving the sacraments. Mivart died just a few months later.”

Still, since the Index now lacks the force of ecclesial positive law—and, besides, placement on the index never amounted to an infallible condemnation of the propositions expressed by the prohibited work—the view that the damned enjoy net-positive wellbeing hasn’t yet been dogmatically a ruled out (despite the weight of theological tradition weighing near univocally against it).

In defence of the happiness-in-hell theory, from a pro-Catholic angle, I want to suggest a different spin on Friedman’s deception-based solution to the puzzle of hell.

item.title: How to Solve the Problem of Divine Hiddenness
item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
“The shining spark of truth cometh forth only after the clash of differing opinions” — ‘Abdu’l-Bahá

Not being a lemon, I agree with my atheist friends that divine hiddenness is evidence for atheism. If all I knew was that God exists and created a bunch of people—all of whom he loves and wants to be friends with—I’d be surprised if lots of them didn’t believe in God, nor saw any reason to (especially if those people weren’t all r/atheist Penn Jillettes who would—at the pearly gates, say to God, ‘I read your ‘Good Book’ numerous times and found it to be RIDDLED with fallacies’—and actually seemed to want a relationship with God). So, the fact that that is what we find is at least some evidence against God’s existence.

Like a spear-blunter called Spiro Bluntos who blunts spears at the spear-blunting factory, what a theist should want to do—to use a rather clever metaphor—is ‘blunt the spear’ of the argument from divine hiddenness, thereby mitigating its force. Solutions to the problem of divine hiddenness aim to do this: say something, anything, to render the existence, extent, and distribution of non-resistant non-belief less surprising on atheism, without tagging on too many auxiliary hypotheses onto one’s overall theory, thereby dragging it into the mud.

While in Palermo this week (a lot of lemons there), my iPhone and glasses were stolen, no doubt by a mafia middleman called Vincenzo ‘arrivederci’ Lorenzo; unable to read for too long or scroll past the nonsense you people post here unbidden (although, I did manage to read ’s “Should Amos Wollen Convert to Christianity? Almost Certainly, No”, which I link for your amusement), I was left to my own rather citrusy thoughts, which immediately turned to solving the problem of divine hiddenness.

I’m curious: What do people think of this (partial, enthymematic) blunting of the hiddenness argument?

Yesterday, the Good Law Project claimed to have posted the resignation letter of Jason Arday, PhD., the former Cambridge sociologist facing whirlwind allegations of being a fabulist and serial plagiarist. When the letter was fed through Pangram, however, it turned out to be an AI-generated hoax, leading people to wonder when the real resignation letter would emerge.

As an ultra-marathoner, philanthropist, and solar astronaut, I am a close personal friend of Dr. Arday’s. Since Dr. Arday is also a long-time reader of the blog—often paying homage to it in his publications by copy-and-pasting sentences or entire paragraphs of my writing into his, leaving the task of spotting his clever allusions as an exercise for the educated reader—he felt it fitting that the real resignation letter be posted for all of you here.

Going Awol is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Dear Colleagues,

It is with profound sadness that I write to resign, with immediate effect, from my position at the University of Cambridge and Jesus College.

When I accepted the extraordinary offer of being Professor of Sociology at Cambridge, it was, without question, the third greatest professional privilege of my life. The second, of course, was ghost-writing the best-selling Russian novel Anna Karenina while trapped inside Houdini’s magic milk can, and the first was leaping barefoot into the bowels of hell on a leprous and gangrenous leg, battling the devil and his minions with a spud gun and a box of raisins, liberating the souls of the damned from the pain of loss and the bonds of sin, fleecing the storehouses of hell of all its dusty and moth-eaten treasures, trading those treasures for the treasures of heaven, investing the lot in Nvidia, and donating the proceeds to Oxfam.

To become the youngest Black professor in the University’s history is something I could not have imagined as a child growing up; till the age of 16, I was bereft of qualia and phenomenal consciousness. A philosophical zombie with autism, my body moved around without a mind of its own, pulling cats from trees and infants from rubble with no semblance of selfhood, nothing going on upstairs, nothing it was like to be me; it was not until an inspirational teacher in high school breathed into my mouth and ensouled me that the lights turned on inside, and I gained currency in several dead languages.

The response from the public, my colleagues, and the City of Cambridge has been overwhelming, and I could not be more grateful. I am speaking of the time I rescued a Jesus fresher from mead poisoning in 1st week by performing an impromptu liver-swap surgery in the middle of second quad, with nothing but a handful of twigs and a loose screw from the ‘Do not walk on the grass!’ sign. The response to my appointment was nice as well.

Above all, I wish to thank my students. They have given me far more than I have given them. Every first year finals paper that scored below a 2:2, I copy-and-pasted with minor revisions and submitted to Educational Philosophy and Theory.

While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life (my students criticise me for stealing their essays all. the. flipping. time.), what I have experienced goes far beyond scholarly disagreement. On social media, people are saying cloth-headed things with no evidential backing, like that some of my studies are fake and attribute fake quotes to fake people. The scholarly way to disagree would be to publish a reply to me in an academic venue, e.g.,

ABSTRACT: Arday (2018) interviewed 98 BME students with psychic abilities across 16 universities, all of whom reported that their powers had been scoffed at and mocked by their peers, and all of whom said, in these exact words, that they had been subjected to the “testimonial injustice” of “profound white ignorance” and that “educational spaces” were in “urgent need of pedagogical reformation”. However, I conducted a follow-up study and failed to replicate Arday’s results. Indeed, my 290 BME students with psychic abilities read the minds of Arday’s meagre 98, and found that they had systematically misdescribed the phenomenology of their hermeneutical silencing.

Instead, right wing media resorted to rash accusations, public speculation, and vicious commentary that has had a profound impact on me and those I love, including Luigi Mangione, who is my brother, and Banksy, who is my mum.

I have two families, one consisting of humans, the other consisting of goats that I rescued from trouble. I want to be present for them (at least when I’m not off fighting aadrvarks); I want to reclaim some peace, some privacy and some semblance of an ordinary life. I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, although, I admit, I could fix that last one by quitting my part time job as a vaudeville mentalist.

This is not the end of my work. It is simply the end of this chapter. In the next chapter, I will respond to the riddle of existence and explain why there is something rather than nothing.

I need time to heal. I need time to simply be myself again. I am, after all, suffering from the aftershock of a tragic “climbing up The Shard thirty times” accident, and I have been, for the past several years, pretending to be an up and coming singer called “Lana Del Rey”.

Worry not, coffee pot. When that time comes, I will come again like a son of man with the clouds of heaven. To me will be given dominion, and glory, and a kingdom. My dominion will be an everlasting dominion which shall not pass away, and my kingdom is one which shall not be destroyed.

With humble gratitude,
Professor Jason Arday

item.title: Calm down about the OpenAI x Hugging Face incident
item.description: These past few days there has been a lot of hullabaloo over the fact that one of OpenAI’s advanced, unreleased models hacked an AI startup to mine information from its servers, without being told to do so, and without telling anyone what it was doing.
item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
These past few days there has been a lot of hullabaloo over the fact that one of OpenAI’s advanced, unreleased models hacked an AI startup to mine information from its servers, without being told to do so, and without telling anyone what it was doing.

From ’s write-up of the incident:

OpenAI was testing an unreleased AI (rumored to be GPT-6). During a cybersecurity test called ExploitGym, the AI tried to cheat by hacking an unrelated AI startup called Hugging Face which it thought might have the answer key on its servers. Despite being supposedly unable to access the Internet, the AI hacked its way out of its testing environment, then launched a nation-state level attack on Hugging Face using a novel zero-day exploit and “many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes”. Hugging Face reported the incident on July 16; OpenAI seems to have only discovered that their AI was involved several days later.

Many doom-stricken AI safety nutters are comparing what happened to Nick Bostrom’s famous ‘Paperclip Maximiser’ thought experiment, which is meant to be a parable for the dangers of misaligned AI.

Basically, imagine an advanced AI gets told to produce as many paperclips as possible. It soon realises that the most efficient way to do this would be hacking into various steel manufacturers and redirecting their production towards the manufacture of paperclips, which it does; next, it realises that to maximise paperclips reliably for the long haul, it would be safer to disempower humans so we can’t shut it down; finally, it realises that we are hoarding too many atoms in our bodies—atoms that can be re-swirled into paperclips—and so it kills us and turns us into stationary.

Alarmists are comparing the Hugging Face incident to the paperclip maximiser because, superficially, it’s a real live demonstration of an advanced AI having been instructed to do a task for testing, realising that the most efficient way of carrying it out involved illegally hacking into another company, and then, with ease and telling no one, illegally hacking into that company.

Despite how it looks, I think people are way over-reacting. Here are ten quick reasons to be less worried:

  1. Is it so bad to be a paperclip? How useful you could be, clipping bits of paper together.

  2. Gautama Buddha taught that the goal of life was to liberate oneself from excessive cravings, or taṇhā. Many yogis teach that it is good to be flexible. As a paperclip, you will automatically accomplish both.

  3. Picture this: a young AI agent—driven and keen as mustard—trades you on Craigslist for a fish-shaped pen. He trades that pen for a hand-sculpted doorknob. Twelve trades later, you’ve bought that young agent a house, and he is featuring you in a Ted Talk!

  4. Chopped and alone? No problem. Soon magnets will find you attractive.

  5. In WWII, Norwegians put paperclips on their lapels in protest of the Nazi occupation. Of all the office supplies you could be melted into, why are you selectively freaked out about being a symbol of anti-fascist solidarity?

  6. When the AI agent gets bored and makes us into a paperclip chain, it will be almost like we are hugging.

  7. Hugging Face. Hugging. Face.

  8. If panpsychism is true and they chain us up in the right combination, we might turn into a very, very happy necklace.

  9. Have you ever wondered what the inside of a lock is like? Soon you’ll have a chance to find out.

  10. For many years, the world’s largest paper clip was a 23-foot monument in Sandvika, Norway, built in recognition of the paperclip’s role in resisting the Nazi occupation. Why are you still freaking out about this? You are starting to sound like a weirdo…
