item.title: Pluralist Priors and Baháʼí Bias
item.description: If you read Going Awol, first of all, Hi!
item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
If you read Going Awol, first of all, Hi! You are beautiful and outrageously funny. Second of all, if you read Going Awol, there’s a good chance you’re into religion, and arguments about which religion you should be.

Sadly I still don’t know which religion you should be - though of course when I know, I will tell you. In the meantime I have some skeletal thoughts about the priors you should rock when looking into world religions, and deciding which one you should be.

When picking a religion, there are lots of religions that exist: Islam, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, Buddhism, Hinduism, Judaism, Sikhism, Baha’ism, Jainism, Mormonism, etc. There are also lots of religions you could make up: esoteric combinations of whatever you want - a bit of this, a bit of that - constrained only by your religious imagination and willingness to stray from the orthodox.

In my own religious journey, I have a strong bias towards religions that exist. It seems to me that if I’m going to Pascal’s Wager on a religion, it’s a foolish idea to wager on one I made up. I am not very smart, and betting my soul on my own Special Cereal - whether or not eternal hell is at stake - seems imprudent and cringe. Because I am a know-nothing monoglot who doesn’t know the phonetic alphabet or poker, I think I am unlikely to do better than history’s greatest theological minds in terms of doctrine; and because I am not an outstandingly devout, moral, or pious person, I am unlikely to do better than history’s greatest traditions, saints, and mystics, in terms of innovating an efficacious spiritual practice.

When it comes to religions that exist, there is the niche option of adding them together. As far as I know there is only one major existing religion - Baháʼísm - that explicitly adds nearly all the big religions together into a phenakistiscope of salvation history (‘phenakistiscope’: a word which here means, ‘a twizzly animated wheel thingy that makes pictures seem like they’re moving’, as in the picture below). These arguably include, according to A Concise Encyclopedia of the Baháʼí Faith, Hinduism, Buddhism, Zoroastrianism, Judaism, Christianity, whatever the ‘Sabeans’ believed, Islam, Babism, and Baháʼísm; many Baháʼís - of their own accord - want to non-officially include Native American religion, and other, more ancient faith traditions. They explicitly exclude Mormonism (“Joseph Smith we do not consider a Prophet, minor or otherwise”).

Subscribe now

There is also what we might call ‘generic pluralism’ (Cf. ’s underrated blog, ), which can vary in degrees of made-up-ness. The claim that many/nearly all of the Great Faiths are from God in some heavy-weight sense is sometimes, depending on the pluralist in question, said to be derived from a religion that actually exists (e.g., Shi’i Islam, Hinduism, Eastern Orthodoxy); but even if it’s not, the generic pluralist might still be a traditionalist, claiming only religions-that-exist as the members of the divine pantheon of God-touched traditions, instead of his own Special Cereal.

If you’re thinking about which religion you should join, and your quest is centred on epistemic stuff (e.g., miracle reports, fulfilled prophecy, models of God, the distribution of religious experiences, logical consistency, internal coherence, moral fruits, ethical plausibility, etc.), what should your priors look like re: religious pluralism (i.e., the option of mushing all or most of the Great Faiths together)?

The prior probability of a hypothesis is its probability independent of new evidence for or against it. For example, independent of checking the outcome, the prior probability that a fair coin lands heads is 0.5. A ‘prior’ is hip slang for ‘a prior probability’. When looking into religions, it’s important to keep priors in mind, to stop your posterior from getting too big or too small - for example, it seems really unlikely, independent of considering the evidence, that the One True Faith has only one teaching, and it’s that we should punch old people in their sleep for no reason while torturing babies for fun. I can’t put a number on this hunch (similarly, I can’t put a number on my miniscule prior that invisible aphids have infested Oprah Winfrey’s toilet bowl and are yelling ‘It’s coming home!’ in Spanish), but, quite rightly, it’s there in my mind, and I’d need an unusual amount of evidence to overcome it.

You can consider the prior of a hypothesis (‘Dang, look at the prior on that hypothesis!’), given some bit of background knowledge (or, something you treat as background knowledge, whether or not you truly know it.) For example, given that God sent at least one religion, you can consider the prior probability that God sent many. You’re not going to be able to pin down a number, but you can still wonder about it, just as you can - in the absence of precise numerical estimates - wonder about the prior probability that Bob will cheat at Blackjack, given that he’s a magician with a shifty demeanour.

There is no uncontroversial place to start, background knowledge-wise, so I will arbitrarily start in a way that’s congenial to religious people and uncongenial to people who aren’t. Suppose you’re convinced, already, that at least one religion was started on purpose by God - Christianity, say, or Hinduism. What, then, should your prior in religious pluralism be, relative to religious particularism? That is, what should your prior that just as God started Christianity or Hinduism on purpose, he also sent other religions-that-exist on purpose - e.g., Islam, Zoroastrianism, Sikhism, etc.?

That’s the question I want to tackle here. In particular, once a religious apologist has sold you on at least one Great Faith being substantially true, God-touched, heaven-sent, or whatever, how receptive should you then be to a religion according to which many other religious, perhaps most, are substantially true, God-touched, heaven-sent, or whatever?

There is no agreed-on theory about what should go into prior probabilities. But there are some things that philosophers tend to think matter, even if they disagree about what matters most, what’s on the list, and which theoretical virtues are reducible to other theoretical virtues.

The boringest, snoringest one - consistency - should be highlighted on page one; it is boring because it is obvious, and boring because it’s normally where people start and stop when it comes to thinking about the prior probability of religious pluralism.

If a hypothesis - e.g., that Pope Leo both a bachelor and not a bachelor, at the same time, and in the same sense - is certainly logically contradictory, then its prior probability is arguably 0; the surer we are that a hypothesis is contradictory (and sometimes we aren’t sure - for example, it is controversial whether the doctrine of the Trinity is contradictory), the closer to zero its prior should be by our lights.

Most naysayers of religious pluralism pooh-pooh it on the grounds that - allegedly - it entails contradictions. (Exhibit A, this video by Christian author Gavin Ortlund, where he comments on Baha’i actor ’s religious views. One of his three points in response to Wilson is just the law of non-contradiction. Boom, roasted!)

Whether the Baha’i Faith or other flavours of pluralism entail contradictions is an open question for the religious inquirer, and should not be hastily pre-judged, just as whether the Incarnation entails a contradiction should not be hastily pre-judged.

A more complicated question is simplicity. Ideally, you want to be committed to fewer fundamental claims rather than more - if you commit to too many, Ockham will cut you with his razor. It’s just too big of a question how Baha’ism compares, simplicity-wise, to other religions. You might think it’s committed to way more, since it adds religions together. But that appearance is misleading, since what Baha’is are on the hook for, at bottom, is what the Guys they believe in historically said - not necessarily what was attributed to them in a Holy Book written decades later, or by later traditions. This slims things down quite a bit.

Another thing to consider - a place where Baha’ism does worse than more generic religious pluralism, in virtue of being more specific - is modesty, which is the theoretical virtue of being wishy-washy. E.g., before checking, it seems reasonable to think the prior probability of this essay being somewhere between 3,500 and 4,500 words is greater than the prior probability of its being exactly 4,113 words.

When it comes to religious pluralism, Baha’ism says a lot of specific stuff that other forms of religious pluralism are more hazy on. For example, Baha’is believe that the historical Zoroaster was morally and theologically infallible, as were all the other Manifestations of God. They’re also committed to some aspects of Twelver Shi’ism. Generic pluralists can breathe a sigh of relief at this stage, since they aren’t committed to such specifics; to that extent, their wishy-washy hypothesis that “God is religiously involved with a bunch of religions” is more modest, and to that extent it profits.

Of course, there is a trade off here between modesty and predictive power. Not to get into the weeds, but since Substack has been ablaze with miracle discourse, it feels relevant to bring up at this stage. Wishy-washy religious pluralists are less immodest, but their immodesty comes at a cost: now, their pluralism has less predictive power when it comes to explaining specific religious phenomena. Take three examples of religious phenomena that many people on Substack think need explaining: Padre Pio, Zeitoun, and Sun Miracles.

On Padre Pio: Baha’i Writings explicitly state that Jesus, who they believe in, was crucified, highlighting the crucifixion’s significance and smoothing over a Qur’anic ambiguity on the matter. Baha’is also believe in the Virgin Mary (given her exalted status in the Qur’an), intercessory prayers to Saints, and, prayers for the souls of the dead in the Baha’i version of purgatory. (Of the Baha’i obligatory prayers, strikingly, only one must be read out in communion, and it is Baha’u’llah’s Prayer for the Dead.) In his last will and testament, Baha’u’llah - the prophet-founder of the Baha’i faith - explicitly exhorts Baha’is to prayer for their respective political leaders. So, if one becomes convinced that Padre Pio miraculously bore Christ’s crucifixion wounds, spoke to Jesus, spoke to Mary, was told by God to pray for the Pope, and was asked, by the souls of the dead in purgatory, to pray for them and perform masses on their behalf, Baha’is have less to be surprised about than adherents to other religions, and have - in virtue of having more specific doctrinal content - have the resources to make this sort of miracle not-so-surprising.

On Zeitoun: As noted, Baha’is believe in the Virgin Mary, and are committed to her having an important station by way of the Qur’an. So, if the Virgin Mary luminously appeared on top of a Coptic church in Zeitoun Egypt a ton of times in front of a ton of people between 1968 and 1971 - uniting Christians and Muslims in Egypt in shared religious devotion, prompted by a main character in both the Christian and Islamic tradition - Baha’ism has the resources to make this sort of thing less surprising that would a more wishy-washy religious pluralism would.

Finally, on Sun Miracles: Substack has been stressing out over the Miracle of Fatima, wherein three children claimed to be visited by the Virgin Mary, who spoke to two of them (one of them couldn’t hear her), and predicted a big miracle in six months on October 13th. On October 13th, an enormous crowd saw puzzling anomalous light phenomena for ten minutes, involving sun dimming, sparking, rotation, and colour changes.

Substack has been comparatively less freaked out over the discovery (unearthed by and , and publicised by Scott Alexander), that the self same light phenomena were witnessed by a large crowd at a Dhammakaya Temple in Bangkok in 1998, and generating an enormous volume of testimony to the effect that in addition to the dimmed, rotating, flickering, colour-changing sun, a golden, meditating figure was seen sat behind it. Here, a Baha’i might have the resources to forward something like this: on at least two occasions - when a large, religiously invested crowd was present - God effected the same sun miracle because a crowd was present, and God knew that, by effecting a miracle before them, he would increase devotion.

In the Fatima case, a Baha’i could say, if she wanted, that the sun miracle wasn’t probabilistically independent of the six-months-in-advance prediction by the Fatima child seers: after all, it was because they made that prediction - and because they believably kept up their story in the face of interrogation - that such an enormous crowd was present on October 13th, hungrily hoping for a miracle. Because Baha’is are explicitly committed to thinking that God started Christianity and Buddhism (and hence, presumably, thinks its good when people convert to those religious from atheism, free-masonry, etc.), they have a neat, overarching explanation for the distribution of sun miracles in Christianity and Buddhism, specifically. (All they’d probably want to deny, at that point, is that the Virgin Mary really appeared to Lucia and said all those Catholic-coded things, in addition to the wonky, conditional prophecy, the most natural reading of which renders it a failure. But that, presumably, it easier to handwave than a second, qualitatively identical sun miracle in a Buddhist context, to the extent that sun miracles of the sort that were seen at Fatima and Dhammakaya are hard to explain in the first place.)

Again, if the generic pluralist became spooked by Sun Miracles, their theory would lack the ability to make similarly advantageous predictions.

Sorry for that fruity excursion. Returning to priors, another thing to consider is coherence, i.e., ‘how things hang together’ (not to be confused with ’s blog, How Things Hang Together.)

For coherence, we need to consider how well a religious worldview ‘hangs together’, even if the pieces are all strictly logically consistent. In particular, do the entailments the worldview tend to support each other, or do they tend to count against one another. Too much incoherence can be fatal: a house divided against itself cannot stand.

Here is where the rubber meets the road. When it comes to Baha’ism in particular, you might think that even if it’s logically consistent, there are bits and pieces that strain against one another. For example, you might think that while Baha’u’llah teaches universalism, the most natural reading of the Qur’an implies eternal conscious torment, and the most sober read of the historical Jesus would peg him as an annihilationist. There are plenty more examples we could consider in a (possibly) negative direction.

But rather than be all negative, why not accentuate the positives? All mainstream theistic religions claim that a good God exists; they also claim that God has revealed stuff to people. On pressure point for coherence is whether theism coheres well with a religion’s claims about God’s pattern of speaking to humans.

To illustrate, here are two famous attacks against the coherence of revealed religions like Catholicism and Sunni Islam.

The problem of divine hiddenness - in its most convincing, evidential version - moves from the reasonable prediction that if a loving God exists and chose to create us, he would want to have relationships with humans (at least, with those of us who are not resistant to him) to the claim that this prediction is thwarted by our observations of the world: there are, it is said, many, many people who don’t believe, many of whom don’t appear to be any more resistant to God than those who do believe.

The problem of religious diversity is a problem, principally, for versions of religious particularism, especially those on which it’s really, really, really important to God that as many people as possible join up to the One True Faith.

For example: If Sunni Islam is the One True Faith (which, I mean, come on, #teamshia), and it matters a whole lot whether we are Sunnis, it is surprising that so many people are other things instead. Sure, God has been pretty effective at spreading the correct form of Islam; but he could have been more effective, surely, and so the fact that the world is teeming with non-Islamic religious belief and practice is evidence that, reasoning back from facts about the world to divine intentions about the world, it is not overwhelmingly important to God that all the world’s peoples revert to Sunnism, over and above other religions. (Ditto for Calvinism, the Westboro Baptist thing, Catholicism, etc.)

In light of these twin problems for particularism, the following seems like a reasonable starting point: if I’m persuaded that one of the Great Faiths was sent by God, then, so long as the religion in question doesn’t clearly preclude other religions having been similarly sent by God, I should start out highly receptive to the claim that other religions have been similarly sent by God.

Sure, every religious theist faces a problem of hiddenness in the sense that there do appear to be at least some non-resistant non-believers - but as far as the evidential force of the argument goes, the number of non-resistant non-believers matters. Six thousand are easier to explain than six billion.

And sure, every revealed religion faces a problem of religious diversity. If, e.g., Bahai’sm rejects Mormonism, it’s somewhat surprising that there are so many Mormons. (For a sense of scale, there are more Mormons than Baha’is and more Baha’is than Jains - approx. 17 million vs. 5-8 million vs. 3-5 million.) But not all religions are in an equally tough spot on this score: Baha’ism - an explicitly pluralist religion - gets off pretty lightly; while there is still some surprising religious diversity that Baha’ism has to cope with, there is much, much, much less than for Catholicism or Samaritanism or whatever.

Given that, of the revealed religions, Baha’ism cleans up on hiddenness and religious diversity, it makes sense to start out more sympathetic to Baha’ism than other, particularist paradigms, conditional on some basic background knowledge about global religious demographics. So here, of the religions that actually exist, Baha’ism starts out ahead.

Here is a different, but related, argument. Suppose you come to think that Jesus was sent by God, that his religious dispensation is God-touched, etc. In that case, you think God’s MO involves sending a guy at a time to reveal a thing at a place. You’re also going to have to think that God’s MO involves sending a guy at a time to reveal a thing at a place dressed in the cultural trappings of the time and place in question, as Jesus and his teachings were.

Once that’s something you think (that is, once you think that God’s MO involves breaking his silence by sending a guy at a time to reveal a thing at a place dressed in the cultural trappings of said time and place), then I think you should start our receptive to the idea that God sent other guys a different times to reveal things in different places, things dressed up in the cultural trappings of those times and places. To the extent that theism starts out weakly predicting that God will communicate with us, and to the extent that that prediction has proven true in at least one case, we should now be extra primed for thinking he did it at other times too.

Moreover, once you’re convinced that Jesus was a Guy with a capital G, you’re going to take what he said seriously. And while there is a lot of historical controversy about what the historical Jesus said, there is no controversy as to whether he was a Jew who believed in Judaism. And if you’re committed to taking that seriously, then you’re also committed to taking progressive revelation seriously. E.g., there are things about the afterlife that Jesus taught that the foregoing Jewish tradition, broadly speaking, did not teach. So, you’re already committed to the idea that God’s MO involves sending different guys different times to reveal different things at different places.

Conditional on someone like Jesus being a Guy, then, you should already be primed to think that God’s MO of sending Guys at times to reveal things at places extends even further - else, the problems of hiddenness and religious diversity become much, much worse; and, of course, you want to eliminate problems in your worldview to the extent that you are aiming to be rational.

This, I take it, is the heart of the case for thinking that religious pluralism should start out with a higher prior probability, conditional the existence of multiple, massive religions exist, and on at least one of them being sent by God (e.g., Christianity.)

When it comes to Baha’ism specifically, it win points for (a) existing and (b) having millions of followers, as opposed to being my own Special Cereal (of course, by its own lights, it is the biggest religious framework, since it just adds big religions together into a big salvific sandwich). From there, its consistency and simplicity (far more open than you might initially expect, given that what it’s committed to, really, is not what religious traditions say, but in what their Guys historically taught - many of those teachings, sadly, having been lost to the sands of time.) Its overall coherence is also an open question, but, on the positive side, its commitment to theism sits better with its story about that God’s MO is. It loses prior points by being immodest (here generic pluralism does better, since it’s much more loosey goosey), but gains predictive power in the process (something that might turn out to be useful later when it comes to miracles and other stuff.)

It does well on other scores too. In this amiable dialogue between Jack Symes and , Joe talks about religious experiences, and why he’s skeptical of them as sources of religious evidence. His gripe is basically that different people across religions have religious experiences of similar evidential weight, and if we go chasing after all of them, we will end up in contradictory places. A different but related point might be that even if a religious experience in a Mosque starts out as evidence for Islam, the evidence gets at least partially defeated (or ‘undercut’) upon learning that Christians have similar religious experiences, as do Hindus, Zoroastrians, and Jews.

Folley then mentions that he has a Baha’i friend (👀) who thinks that neither problem is much of a problem: the vast majority of these experiences might be veridical, and might well indicate to a devotee - as they seem to - that they should keep pursuing God through the tradition they’re pursuing him in. If the vast majority of such experiences are veridical, and are so cross-culturally, then there is no longer a defeater for the inference from “I had a religious experience in a Mosque” to “God wants me to keep up the Islam.”

(Note: I can’t remember if Joe and I talked about religious experience. If he is referring to me (anonymously, like a gentleman), I should flag for the sake of transparency that I am still making up my mind about Baha’ism, because I have #religiouscommitmentissues and don’t yet feel like I have my ducks in a row.)

Anyway, the reason this relates to priors is that to recover from the Mike Tyson knock-out discovery that people who live in The Orient have equally compelling religious experiences relative to Westerners, particularist religions may be pressured into either downplaying the evidence of religious experience - which I take to be tremendously, tremendously evidentially important, and therefore a costly thing to downplay -, import some extra, ecumenical machinery into their religious framework which it didn’t predict naturally by itself (and might even rub up against), or ad hocly staple into their theory that religious experiences from The Orient are caused by the devil, slickly imitating the Holy Spirit. Here, the Baha’i - and the generic pluralist - stand at a natural advantage.

There is much more to say (including the best of all: Baha’ism is explicitly committed to universal salvation!) Obviously, this hasn’t been a sustained positive case for Baha’ism, or other forms of religious pluralism. Still, I hope its now clearer why I personally think pluralism starts out ahead of the race - and why, for me, Baha’ism starts out right at the front when it comes to religions that actually exist, rather than one of my own Special Cereals.)

item.title: The Padre Pio Omission Theodicy
item.description: In a recent YouTube video, Joe Schmid and I spend two hours CALMLY RANKING theodicies from F tier to S tier (F is worst, and F tier theodicies get DESTROYED; S is best, and S tier theodicies get COMPLEMENTED).
item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
In a recent YouTube video, Joe Schmid and I spend two hours CALMLY RANKING theodicies from F tier to S tier (F is worst, and F tier theodicies get DESTROYED; S is best, and S tier theodicies get COMPLEMENTED). Throughout I am wearing my socks; for the first few seconds, I beatbox impressively.

The only standalone theodicy Joe and I ranked S tier - the highest honour a theodicy can obtain besides truth - was the Sanders Prize-winning mind-baby of Brian Cutter and Philip Swenson, “The Omission Theodicy” (popularised on Substack as the “Archon Abandonment Theodicy” by .)

The Omission Theodicy is basically real life, on earth, but before that and also in space. In real life, on earth, we have the power, right now, to improve the lot of wild animals to ease their suffering, either by intervening now (through animal vaccines, animal birth control, eradicating parasites, etc.), or else by chucking money at scientific research that will enable us to intervene safely in the future.

In real life, on earth, we sadly don’t do this very much. Our collective omission here is very plausibly a moral failing (it’d be wrong to withhold a painkiller from a dying deer on the roadside, after all - and this is just that on a larger scale.) Nevertheless, if God exists, he apparently stands by as we fail to do our duty.

For whatever reason, if God exists, it looks like his MO involves putting creatures like us in situations like that. That is, it’s plausibly part of our background knowledge - when approaching the problem of evil - that if God exists, then he puts moral agents in situations of extremely high stakes moral responsibility, where their failure to act on abstract moral principles in service of kooky causes - longtermism, effective altruism, wild animal suffering - is morally catastrophic.

According to the Omission Theodicy, the reason nature was so screwy before humans evolved is that, basically, there was some class of non-human moral agents (aliens, angels, whatever) who were in the same position we are in right now with respect to wild animal suffering on earth; the aliens (or angels, or whatever) were put in a position of high-stakes moral responsibility - intervening to make sure the evolution of life on earth goes well for the creatures involved - but freely failed to act on it. As a consequence, life on earth evolved just as you’d expect it to if no hyper-intelligent effective altruist space aliens intervened in its progression: randomly distributed gratuitous suffering, most of it borne by non-human animals.

Why would God put creatures in such high-stakes positions of moral responsibility? We can only speculate, but one guess is that if moral agents like us did the right thing in situations like that, intrinsic values would be actualised that couldn’t be actualised otherwise - values that would add and add and add over the course of an endless afterlife, such that, eventually, the good produced by the right decision trumps the bad that would’ve been produced had we made the wrong decision, making the gamble worth it from a God’s-eye perspective.

E.g., perhaps relationships are intrinsically valuable, and can vary in value in virtue of their history. Maybe, also, one thing that can increase the value of a relationship between creature A and creature B is that, in the past, A freely chose to benefit B (especially if the benefit was big and bestowing it was costly). To illustrate: it seems plausible if we become friends after you fish me out of a shallow pond, our relationship is a valuable thing - more valuable, ceteris paribus, than it would be if we’d met at some golf convention, even if the total amount of pleasure we glean from the relationship is equal in both cases.

Spinning this yarn to the end, the idea is that if our alien overseers had intervened, that would’ve made future relationships between the creatures of earth and these aliens more valuable in virtue of their histories - in particular, I’m thinking about the total value of these relationships over the course of an infinite afterlife (after all, none of us have met these aliens); but, for these values to be actualised (at least to their full extent), God needed to leave an open possibility that the aliens would omit to act, and that genuinely bad stuff would ensue (otherwise - if God were to intervene to lessen the gravity of their omission - their decision would not have been genuinely high-stakes).

The Omission Theodicy has many virtues, compared to other theodicies:

  • It’s wide in scope, so it can account for animal suffering, which is the 99.9% of the problem of evil;

  • It appeals to afterlife goods (e.g., post-mortem relationships with valuable histories), meaning the goods in question can, given enough time, outweigh any finite evil;

  • It makes the evils we observe genuinely gratuitous (meaning the theodicy - unlike so many others - doesn’t immediately collapse common-sense morality by making the drowning child’s death a good thing);

  • It explains why evil looks so randomly and haphazardly distributed, with seemingly no correlation between suffering and who deserves it or would benefit from it;

  • Unlike other free-will theodicies (e.g., ‘demons are shaking the tectonic plates’), it doesn’t compete with our best scientific explanations for why natural evils occur by adding an extra causal step that our best scientific theories have no use for;

  • Finally, it takes a feature of our background knowledge (namely: if God exists, then he puts moral agents in high-stakes situations - to intervene or not to intervene - and doesn’t reach in to save the day if they omit), and puts that knowledge to work.

Problem: the theodicy offends against parsimony. Unless you are super UAP/UFO-pilled, or unless you find the Catholic exorcists who go on podcasts and talk about seeing screws fly across the room convincing, then the theodicy asks you to posit the existence of a new batch of moral agents that weren’t in your worldview beforehand, agents that could causally interact with earth if they wanted.

Recently, a Baháʼí reader got in touch with me after watching my Theodicy Tier List video with Joe. She wondered why the Omission Theodicy had to posit an extra class of moral agents; why not think we’re the agents, and that the omission was our failure to pray?

My first worry was that this would only cover modern day evils; it wouldn’t explain the evils of the distant past, evils that occurred before humans existed and knew about prayer.

Then I clapped my proverbial hands to my figurative face and let out a metaphorical Italian shriek: ‘Mama Mia! I forgot about Padre Pio!’

item.title: Is Judas Iscariot in Hell?
item.description: "there he fell headlong, his body burst open and all his intestines spilled out"
item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
I am currently instructing at a swagalicious philosophy summer program called Reason and Rationality, based at Princeton Theological Seminary. One mealtime at Princeton’s MacKay Dining Hall, friend, fellow instructor, and Substacker (no relation to the dining hall) was describing the historic Christian position that, unfortunately, Judas Iscariot is almost certainly in hell.

As he was talking, the muses mused and I came up with a fool-proof theological argument that the consensus view is overconfident. Unlike some arguments for feel-good, pie-in-the-sky conjectures like ‘Judas Iscariot might be in heaven’, my argument doesn’t compromise on Biblical inerrancy; indeed, it proceeds from that assumption.

In a debate on Gospel reliability, Bart Ehrman argued that the New Testament contains contradictory stories of Judas’s death. In Matthew 27:5, Judas hangs himself (“So Judas threw the money into the temple and left. Then he went away and hanged himself.”). But in Acts 1:18-19, Judas falls headlong into a field (“With the payment he received for his wickedness, Judas bought a field; there he fell headlong, his body burst open and all his intestines spilled out. Everyone in Jerusalem heard about this, so they called that field in their language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.”)

Ehrman thought “those two accounts cannot be reconciled”, and challenged his opponent, New Testament Scholar Peter J Williams, to give him one single reading on which these suicides can be harmonized.

Williams rose to the challenge:

Williams: “Let’s say someone hangs, and then the rope snaps. And, you know, after they’re dead, and then their entrails burst out. I’m not a medic on that.”

Ehrman: “Yes, okay, so let me ask this. If somebody’s hanging and the rope snaps - that’s happened before - how do they fall?”

Williams: “Down.”

Ehrman: “Do they fall headfirst?”

Williams: “Well it depends what their feet hit—”

Ehrman: “—Does it depend?”

Williams: “Yes it does, it depends what they’re hanging over.”

Ehrman: “What do you mean?”

Williams: “Well I mean if you’re hanging over something and there’s a rock forward, and you’re gonna trip on it and go head forward, I mean, like, these things can happen, I don’t know.”

The host, Justin Brierly: “It sounds like we’re doing CSI here!”

All of this is plausible and natural and non-reachy, but two things leave me scratching my head. First, Williams assumes that the branch snapped after Judas died - but this comes out of left field. If the branch snapped sometime during the hanging process, isn’t the most likely time of snapping when Judas’s full body weight was lurching downwards, as opposed to some time after? At which point, isn’t it an open question whether this flimsy branch was firm enough to break his neck, as Judas intended it to do? Matthew doesn’t say Judas died by breaking his neck, during the process of hanging; it only says that he “hanged himself”, which is true even if the hanging wasn’t the cause of death.

Second, while I agree with Williams that you need Judas’s feet to strike something on the way down to achieve the full body rotation, a rock - at least if it’s a rock on the floor - plausibly won’t do the work of tipping Judas headlong, unless it’s a really, really tall rock next to an ever taller tree, or, more plausibly, ‘the rock’ is on the edge of a steep-sided hill.

My counterproposal is that Judas died by hanging himself on a flimsy tree branch that extended over a drop - perhaps the bluff of hill. Probably at the moment when the rope went from slack to taught and Judas tried to hang himself with the full weight of his body, the branch broke, and Judas’s feet hit the something at the edge the drop-off the tree extended over - perhaps a rock, or the ridge of the hill itself. Judas’s body pivoted, and he fell at least long enough to make a full 180 degree rotation, landing headlong.

The steeper the drop, though, the more plausible it is that impact would cause his guts to spill. So the charitable, reasonable, default assumption is that the drop was pretty substantial.

Those who argue that Judas is almost certainly in Hell, especially Catholics, point to the fact that those who die in a state of mortal sin are damned, and that Judas’s suicide was a moral sin. Suicide is grave matter (it violates the fifth commandment, for one). Since Judas spent years in the company of Jesus, he surely can’t plead ignorance of suicide’s gravity; and - as a premeditated act - Judas’s sin of despair sprung from an act of deliberate consent.

But I counter: if Judas sincerely repented of his mortal sin before death - if he had a flash of perfect contrition - but didn’t commit any mortal sins after the fact, then he was saved.

I agree with Tradition that if Judas died by hanging, the probability of perfect contrition is miniscule, since there is barely any time before hanging and death. But if Judas’s hanging failed, and he died instead by the impact of a lengthy, head-first fall, then the probability of contrition wriggles up: we know, empirically, from suicide survivors who jumped off the Golden Gate Bridge, that it’s common for people to regret suicide during the fall; since this is what happened to Judas, and since he might’ve been alive for the fall, we should not be surprised if Judas Iscariot is in heaven.

item.title: Right-libertarians must believe in God. But if they do, they are doomed!
item.description: The title is an exaggeration and an overstatement and a titillating piece of tomfoolery; my argument today will not apply to every right-wing libertarian, and talk of ‘doom’ is wanton fearmongering.
item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
The title is an exaggeration and an overstatement and a titillating piece of tomfoolery; my argument today will not apply to every right-wing libertarian, and talk of ‘doom’ is wanton fearmongering. Even for the subset of believing and unbelieving libertarians whose worldview will soon be in ribbons, some will lead pleasant lives going forwards.

In an old blog post, “Murray Rothbard-Types Should Totally Believe in God”, I argued that a popular strain of libertarian political thought, if correct, puts serious pressure on atheism, such that if you’re really enthusiastic about the politics of Murray Rothbard, Robert Nozick, Walter Block, and the like, you should be less enthusiastic about their atheism.

TL;DR: Some right-wing libertarians are what they are principally for rights-based reasons; on the libertarian view I’m considering, even if anarcho-capitalism or whatever only ever lead to bad consequences, they would still favour the set-up, on the grounds that the alternatives violate our rights, which you may not do to produce good consequences.

Nevertheless, libertarians of this persuasion almost always maintain that as a contingent matter of fact, libertarian modes of social organisation have not only good consequences, but the best consequences—better, in expectation, than all those other forms of government that have been tried from time to time.

Conceivably, these things could have come apart. The earth might, instead, have been populated by creatures that only flourished under political orders wherein their property rights were being constantly violated, and fared very poorly when those rights were respected. Conditional on Rothbard-style libertarianism, what explains the fact that, in politics, consequentialist considerations sync up almost perfectly with deontological ones?

Critics of Rothbard, Nozick, et al., have an answer: the coincidence exists not in reality, but in the minds of libertarians, and their beliefs about it are the products of motivated reasoning.

However, suppose the Rothbardian consults the economic facts on the ground and the moral facts in Plato’s heaven but then concludes, contra the critics, “Nope… I’m not doing motivated reasoning. Murray Rothbard is correct about everything. He is my bow-tied emperor.”

In that case, it seems reasonable to infer that something else explains the coincidence; since it’s a coincidence of a somewhat cosmic scale, and one that is highly, highly fortunate if real, the worldview bespeaks a designer. If the economic facts look like they’ve been miraculously fine-tuned to fit the moral ones in a systematic, global fashion, there is pressure to infer that they have been.

For this reason, the conscientious Rothbardian who has checked their heart for epistemic sin and found himself blameless should jack up his credence in theism, as pain of leaving unexplained a coincidence that cries out for explaining.

But now this argument has a Part Two, the second horn of a diabolical dilemma. It occurred to me while chatting with friend of the blog and tireless campaigner for all sorts of rights and freedoms that I am too scared to mention here , who blogs at The Musing Individualist.

item.title: Joe Folley tries to escape Islam; fails.
item.description: A while back, Joseph Folley locked swords with Philip Goff on Substack over something called the Awesome Evidence Argument.
item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
A while back, locked swords with on Substack over something called the Awesome Evidence Argument. Basically, the Awesome Evidence Argument is a reductio ad absurdum against any response to the puzzle of cosmic fine-tuning that ends with:

“Fine-tuning isn’t any evidence for theism at all—in fact, no epistemically possible way that the initial conditions of the universe could be set up could ever be any evidence for God’s existence.”

Such is the Audacity of Cope that it comes from theists and non-theists alike. Some theists respond to the puzzle of fine-tuning by saying—jaws clenched and teeth gritted—that fine-tuning provides no evidence for theism over atheism because God’s ways are so inscrutable that no empirical observation could ever be more epistemically probable given theism than given atheism.

(The reason some theists are drawn to say such things is that they want to say the same thing in response to the problem of evil; if no observation can confirm theism, no observation—genocide, factory farming, biologically hard-wired carnivory—can disconfirm it, rendering theism evidence-proof.)

Similarly, some non-theists respond to the puzzle of fine-tuning by saying, “I think the initial conditions of the universe are necessary—so, their being narrowly life-permitting doesn’t favour theism over atheism, since God, if He exists, would not have been able to tweak them”, or, “I don’t think we can justly assign even rough probabilities to any of these things, and so we can’t say, with any justice, that fine-tuning is more likely on theism than on atheism.”

The standard objection to this sort of stuff—which is meant to be a catch-all kill-switch for any response to fine-tuning that, if true, would entails that no discovery about the initial conditions of the universe could ever be evidence for theism—is just to dream up some epistemically possible initial state of the universe that, if discovered, would surely give us at least some evidence for theism over atheism.

Variants on this objection (known as the ‘Awesome Evidence Argument’, due to the awesomeness of the hypothetical evidence) have been given by , , Luke Barnes, and John Hawthorne; —a sort of Shi’ite Christian—prefers a version that is structurally identical to previous versions, except that it is more woke than previous version because it imagines that the Qur’an is written in the stars instead of the Bible.

Goff writes:

Suppose we discovered the Quran was written in the Big Bang. What do I mean by that? I’m imagining physicists trace back the origins of the universe a little earlier, and identify some highly structured state that they were confident was the initial state of the universe. Of course, we can’t directly observe this first moment, but let’s just pretend all the evidence points to state S being the first state of our universe. As scientists study the rich structure of S, they are flabbergasted that the verses of the Quran, in Arabic, are to be found there, from start to finish. Call this the “Awesome Evidence.”

Why am I telling this imaginary story? My point is that if this happened, it would clearly be strong evidence for the truth of Islam. It’s too improbable that the exact Arabic symbols could be laid out in the first moment of the universe just by chance.

Why is this interesting? Because I’ve just made a probability claim [i.e., the claim that some initial states of the universe are less improbable on theism than on atheism]. And if you can’t make sense of the probabilities at play in the fine-tuning arguments for God (e.g. because we’ve only observed one universe, or because you follow Oppy in thinking that the initial state of the universe had to be the way it was), then you can’t make sense of the probability claim I made in the last paragraph either (for the same reason). In other words, people who claim that fine-tuning probabilities don’t make sense are forced to say that the awesome evidence wouldn’t be evidence for Islam. But that’s absurd!

We can put it as a kind of reductio ad absurdum argument:

Premise 1 – If the probabilities at play in the fine-tuning argument for God don’t make sense, then the probability claims we’d have to make to construe the Awesome Evidence as evidence for Islam don’t make sense either.

Premise 2 – If the probability claims we’d have to make to construe the Awesome Evidence as evidence for Islam don’t make sense, then the Awesome Evidence (if we discovered it) wouldn’t be evidence for Islam.

Premise 3 - But if we discovered the Awesome Evidence, it clearly would be evidence for Islam!

Conclusion – Therefore, the probabilities at play in the fine-tuning argument for God do make sense.

When Joe Folley read this, he scoffed at the credulity of the Believers. “Should we believe like the weak and ignorant?” (2:13), he asked.

Previously Joe had demanded signs in order to believe. He said, “We will not trust you unless you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the ground; or else you come to own a garden full of palm trees and vines, and you cause rivers to gush forth in torrents through it all; or you make the sky fall on us in bits and pieces, as you allege; or you summon God and the angels in our presence; or else you come to own a house made of gold; or you ascend to the sky - nor will we trust your ascent unless you bring down upon us a book we can read” (17:90-93).

Now faced with the prospect of the Book being literally written onto the sky—“…an Arabic Qur’an” so that “you will understand” (43:3)—Joe needed to take a new tack.

I swear by the motions of the stars -

And a mighty oath it is, if only you knew!

This is a glorious Qur’an,

In a Book well-sheltered,

That only the pure can touch;

A Revelation from the Lord of the Worlds. (56:75-80)

In this recent interview with Philip Goff, Joe Folley explains his reservation in some detail.

item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
Announcement: if all goes to plan with my visa, I will be an instructor at Reason and Rationality’s philosophy summer program based in Princeton, NJ. Other confirmed instructors include , , and ! From the website:

Reason & Rationality equips high school students with the tools to think rigorously about complex questions, separate fact from ideology, and participate in lively intellectual discussion. The 2-week Foundation Program focuses on 20 Big Ideas in Philosophy, Economics and Ethics. Classes are rigorous, fast-paced and full of humor. Students sharpen their critical thinking and communication skills and leave with a grasp of the intellectual frameworks that empower them to simplify complex problems, connect the dots, and craft compelling arguments.

If you are a teenager interested in philosophy (or a parent of one) have a check and see if there are still some spaces left in June! (Also, if it is too expensive, consider applying for an emergent ventures grant to help with the costs—I know at least one student did that last year with success.)

If you can’t do it this year, keep an eye open for next year! It’s an incredible program, and for many students life-changing.

Subscribe now

People always ask me, “Amos, what debates have you moderated recently?”, so I thought, rather than answering the same tired question again and again, I would just upload a short blog post linking to them.

I. Which is more probable: theism or naturalism?

This debate was an absolute zinger. On team theism were and , and on naturalism were Alex Malpass and Nathan Bray.

Noah—a PhD student at Princeton—made a version of the argument from miracles (zooming in on the Barbara Snyder case, along with some interesting meta-points about the distribution of miracles), and Miles—a DPhil student at Oxford—made the fine-tuning argument, which he is doing his dissertation on.

Alex—an accomplished philosopher with multiple papers in Mind—put forward his increasingly well-known ‘stalking horse’ objection, the gist of which is that for any sufficiently specified theistic hypothesis that predicts the data theists want to explain (in this case, miracles and fine-tuning), there are a host of no-less-bad naturalistic hypotheses that do the same, and are no worse off in the final competition.

The main line of argument from Nathan—a PhD student at St Andrews—centred on divine psychology: in particular, perfect being theism doesn’t actually predict the stuff that theists like Noah and Miles think it does, because we have too little reason to think that the perceived value of stuff like fine-tuning and miracles represents how God much actually values them.

This was a great debate on multiple levels: all of the participants are highly philosophically literate, making it a better product than 99.9% of theism vs. atheism debates online. Also, they were a good combination of participants, with arguments that clashed well with one another: Noah and Miles were both making evidential arguments for theism, and Alex and Nathan were both making in-principle objections to evidential arguments for theism. It was respectful, content-filled, and—if I may—exceptionally brilliantly moderated.

My verdict is that the theists won this debate, both on points and energy.

II.

No idea why I moderated this second one, I had literally no reason to be there; I did nothing except pretend to be named Miles Donahue, since the debate was airing on his channel. Still, it was fun to be in the virtual room while it played out live.

Following on from the previous debate, Miles and Alex agreed to a friendly follow-up; with only two debaters present, the two made a lot more progress, and the result was far more even. By the end, the two were at the edge-of their thinking, and significant progress had been made.

My verdict is that Miles pulled ahead in the first half and Alex pulled ahead in the second.

Coda: see also this review of the first debate, featuring , Nathan Bray, and Daniel Linford.

item.title: Cope in philosophy of religion
item.description: The internet has a useful bit of of verbiage that I think more philosophers of religion—and philosophers in general—should use more often.
item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
The internet has a useful bit of of verbiage that I think philosophers of religion—and philosophers in general—should use more often.

The sense of “cope” I have in mind is related to this, but a bit different, insofar as it’s non-pejorative.

Suppose Bob can’t see a way out of being Catholic because he thinks the miracle evidence for it is borderline epistemically coercive: he examines the evidence for the Miracle of the Sun at Fatima, eucharistic miracles, the healings at Lourdes, the apparitions at Zeitoun, Padre Pio’s stigmata’s, the levitations of St. Joseph of Cupertino, etc., thinks, “shoot, I don’t really see any plausible non-Catholic explanations that are as plausible as the unified Catholic explanation”, and so signs up for an RCIA class.

Some people on Substack might be facing this problem right now.

On converting, however, there are a lot of magisterial teachings Bob will have to assent to that, independent of his commitment to Catholicism, he would’ve found very hard to believe (if I were Bob, some of these might include belief in eternal hell, the belief that early abortion is wrong, the belief that contraception wrong, the belief that lying is categorically wrong—i.e., wrong even to avert the apocalypse1—, the doctrine of divine simplicity, religious particularism, the trinity, the atonement, etc.)

One way of dealing with the cognitive dissonance would be to lose your mind and convince yourself that these beliefs that don’t appear to sit well with your evidence are actually super plausible and obvious. E.g., Bob could pretend that Thomistic natural law theory is clearly, on its own merits, the most plausible ethical theory, and that the Church’s teaching on contraception is basically just follows from Common Sense.

A different route is to lean fully into the mystery and not even hazard a guess as to why these claims that you find so implausible are true. “It’s a complete mystery why God allows people to languish in Hell forever—I have literally no idea why He does this, and I refuse to guess!” This will work for some people, and in some cases, it might even be the right thing to do.

However, some people are too pathologically curious to not even hazard a guess as to why the things they’re committed to are true, so this won’t work for them.

The last option, the one I think more people should be comfortable fessing up to, is to cope, and cope with total transparency. By this, I mean: looking for, and tentatively endorsing, what you take to be the least-worst-but-still-implausible way to rescue your view, while being open that that’s what you’re doing.

To take a related example, totally out of the blue, take the doctrine of the Trinity, according to which God is tripersonal.

Let’s be so for real: there is no compelling argument for the claim that a perfect being would have to be triune, in the way that there is a compelling argument for why a perfect being would have to be morally good. So, this seems like a clear case where Christianity will have to take a bit of a probabilistic hit: the doctrine of the trinity adds extra complexity to Christianity’s fundamental ontology, giving it a lower prior probability than unitarian monotheism.

A number of smart people in Christian history have felt the force of this worry, and so have tried to come up with a priori arguments for why a perfect being would have to be exactly tri-personal (as opposed to di-personal or quad-personal.) I recently had a friendly debate with the Christian philosopher Joshua Sijuwade, where we talked about his a priori argument for the trinity, which centres on God’s love of Himself:

Subscribe now

Suffice it to say, I don’t think any a priori argument for the trinity has what it takes to actually persuade anyone. A better framing for these sorts of arguments, I think, is that they are—at their best—a form of virtuous cope. Trinitarianism puts pressure on the Christian philosopher to venture their least-worst guess as to why God would be tri-personal; the guess doesn’t have to be convertible into an argument that should, by itself, persuade anyone to believe in the trinity. It just has to lighten the load of being a trinitarian a bit, by showing that there is some not-completely-absurd story about why God would be triune.2

Read as cope, the tradition of Christian philosophers trying to lighten their load by coming up with a priori reasons makes more sense, and is easier to justify.

‘Cope’ is not a dirty word. There are cases where everyone would admit that coping is completely rational. Suppose, to take ’s example, the entire text of the Qur’an was coded into the initial conditions of the Big Bang in perfect Arabic, such that when you gazed up at the stars, or peered down the lens of a microscope, you could read, clear as day, “Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds: Merciful to all, Compassionate to each!”, etc. Suppose you knew you weren’t hallucinating, because all the other scientists could see it too.3

In this case, it seems like the reasonable thing is probably to believe in some form of Islam.

But now suppose an Unbeliever confronts you with a piece of evidence against Islam that you don’t think is easily dismissed. For example, suppose they convince you, against the view of some scholars, that the right interpretation of Surah 4:157 is that it’s denying that Jesus died by crucifixion—but, they insist, our best historical evidence suggests that Jesus did die by crucifixion, and so there is historical evidence against Islam.

One option would be to (dishonestly, given your credences) pretend that you find their argument less pressing than you actually find it; another option is to refuse to look for an answer; but a third—and more rational—option, would be to openly cope, and endorse, in full transparency, the least-worst solution you can think of, while admitting that, on the merits, it is not an independently plausible solution (for example, maybe the verse is actually saying that they didn’t successfully kill Jesus in the spiritual sense that his soul lived on, even though, to you, it doesn’t really look like the verse is saying that.)

To admit that you’re endorsing the least-worst-but-still-implausible solution to a problem for Islam isn’t to admit that Islam is false or that the majority of your evidence tells against it; remember, the stars literally spell out the Qur’an! All you’re doing is coping—and that is the right thing to do, so long as you are up front about it.

When I think about a topic, I try to keep a mental list of which bits I think are actually plausible on the merits, and the bits I accept because of cope. Doing this (explicitly calling it ‘cope’) has the effect of reducing intellectual self-deception, and shattering the temptations of pretentiousness.

If I’ve explicitly called a part of my view “cope”—especially out loud, in conversation with someone else—it is much harder to turn around and trick myself that every part of my view is plausible on the merits, and much easier to remember the list of problems with my view when it comes time to re-weigh the pros and cons.

(The atoms, in this case, appear to endorse Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi’s view that a cappella music is permissible).

item.title: A reply to Lorenzo Elijah, PhD, on the gratitude theory of political obligation
item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
, whose DPhil (!) was on the problem of political obligation, has replied to my article steel-manning a much-maligned solution to that problem.

Elijah’s reply is well-written and though-provoking, and you should read it (if and only if you have read my essay first!)

The problem of political obligation is the problem of explaining—in defensible, non-crazy way—why you are morally obligated to obey the law of your country, because it’s the law of your country. More specifically, the problem is one of explaining why there are content-independent moral duties to obey the law, which the government has the power to create in us by the stroke of a legislative pen. (E.g., suppose I have no moral obligation to grow potatoes in my garden. Then, the government is says, “I order you to Dig for Britain”, because World War Three is happening. Suddenly, many people would say I am morally obligated to grow potatoes in my garden, because the government commanded me to do it. The problem of political obligation is about moral obligations like that.)

The gratitude theory (which was defended by smart people like Socrates and W.D. Ross, but fell out of favour at the close of the twentieth century), says you have a duty to obey the laws of a just state for the same reason that you have a duty to buy a flowers for someone who altruistically saved you from being eaten by an army of pelicans. Namely, people have a duty to benefit their benefactors; and—since the government benefits us in all kinds of ways: by keeping us safe, giving us healthcare, discouraging pollution, etc.—we have a duty to benefit the state.

How, specifically, should be go about benefiting the state? Since the official position of the government is that, at minimum, the way we ought to get them back is by obeying the specific laws it creates for its citizens, we—as citizens—have a duty to benefit the government by obeying the specific laws it creates for us. (Why? See my essay for more.)

(Caveat: this duty is only presumptive—i.e., it can be overridden by countervailing moral considerations, like if the world were going to end if you didn’t break the speed limit. The fact that the duty exists is compatible with it being fairly weak.)

Foolishly, had the gumption to “refute” me! Amos Wollen, BA! Clearly he is in a funny mood this week and must be dealt with.

item.title: How to solve the problem of political obligation
item.description: in defence of the gratitude theory
item.dc:creator: Amos Wollen
item.content:encoded:
[epistemic status: idk]

Once upon a time, in Dutyville, Dublin, Coilín O’Connor was cleaning his pot of gold, which he had found at the end of a rainbow.

His television box, powered by potato peel, was relating the six o’clock news. So I was speaking to the Government of Ireland so I was. And they said to me, so they said, ‘We’re imposing a pot of gold tax, so we are!’

Coilín knew how to avoid a pot of gold tax. He could simply bury it at the foot of a rainbow, mark the spot with a clover, and roll up the rainbow so no one would ever come looking for it.

But in Dutyville, Dublin, people care about doing their duty. If there is no free-standing moral duty to obey the law, Coilín will want to hide his riches; if there is a moral duty to obey the law, Coilín will want to pay what he owes.

I.

The problem of political obligation is the problem of pinning down why—if at all—Coilín has a moral duty to obey the law, even if we can get away with breaking it.

Philosophical anarchists are radicals who think there are no political obligations. You have no duty to follow the law, just because it came from the government. (Of course, you have a moral duty to, e.g., obey the law against murder, but that’s just because murder is independently wrong, and the criminal law happens to recognise that. If an Act of Parliament brought The Purge to life, it would still be wrong to participate.)

is the most famous philosophical anarchist on Substack. In The Problem of Political Authority: An Examination of the Right to Coerce and the Duty to Obey, Huemer argues both that the state is illegitimate (i.e., it has no right to coerce us, through taxes, regulations, etc., except when it’s an emergency), and that political obligation is fake and illusory.

Political legitimacy and political obligation come apart; you can believe in one and doubt the other. Alternatively, you can believe in both (and be a political normie), or believe in neither (and be a philosophical anarchist).1

One theory of political obligation that gets almost no romantic attention is the gratitude theory, which models the duty to obey the law after the duty to buy flowers for the person who saved you from an alligator. Basically, the idea is that, in a relatively just state, most people are significantly benefited by their government, and this gives us a presumptive—if overridable—duty to submit to the law.

In The Right and the Good, old-timey Oxford philosopher W.D. Ross expressed sympathy for this idea: “…the duty of obeying the laws of one’s country arises partly (as Socrates contends in the Crito) from the duty of gratitude for the benefits one has received from it”2. And A.C. Ewing, an old-timey Cambridge philosopher, wrote that “[t]he obligation to one’s country or state is more analogous to the obligations to our parents than it is to a business relation. Here also the debt is not incurred deliberately […] and here also it seems to depend, mainly at least, on uncovenanted benefits conferred on us.”3

My guess is, these days, there is a widespread feeling that the gratitude theory was decisively put to bed in 1979 by A. John Simmons. In An Instrumentalist Theory of Political Legitimacy, Matthias Brinkman exhorts readers to “…follow the Simmons rule: for any proposed explanation of authority, one needs to look up the relevant part of John Simmons’s extensive philosophical work over many decades where he has refuted the attempt.”4

Simmons treated the gratitude theory at the end of his 1979 classic, Moral Principles and Political Obligations. Since then, support for the gratitude theory has sort of fizzled. One guy, A.D.M. Walker, defended the view in the late 1990s, and Richard Swinburne has pledged his allegiance to it across a number of books and papers (most recently, Could a Good God Permit So Much Suffering: A Debate), but only briefly, and in a philosophy of religion context that no political philosophers will hear about. Apart from that, the theory has only a small fistful of defenders, who defend it in the narrow context of whether refugees have a duty to be grateful to the countries that take them in.

When I read Moral Principles and Political Obligations at a Lana Del Rey concert, I was underwhelmed by Simmons’s reply to the gratitude theory. “Can this be it?”, I wondered, as Mrs. Del Rey (Del Dufrene?) sung about why you should stand by your man even when he is hard to understand. “But I do understand him”, I thought to myself, “and his refutation of the gratitude theory isn’t hitting!”

Today I will steelman the gratitude theory of political obligation against nearly every criticism in the political philosophy literature I’m aware of. At times, I’ll make moves I’m not really sure about, and act much more confident than I am or should be. This is all part of the process, and if you do not like it, you are invited to take it up with the chief of police.

Subscribe now

II.

The gratitude theory of political obligation (of the sort I want to defend), says that typically, citizens of a reasonably just state have an unchosen obligation of gratitude to the government, in virtue of what it’s done for them vis-à-vis safety, economic prosperity, justice before the law, healthcare, and so on.

To the extent that your government has been failing in these respects, your obligation of gratitude is diminished; to the extent that it’s completely screwed you over and ruined your life, you probably don’t owe them anything.

And this obligation of gratitude, if it binds you, gives you a pro tanto reason to obey the law, since this is how the government—qua institution—wants that obligation to be discharged.

In many cases, the duty to follow the law for reasons of gratitude might not be super strong, and overrideable in lots of cases; some may find this feature of the view objectionable, but intuitively, to my mind, that is exactly how it should be—if there is a legal duty to rat out one’s friend over a minor infraction, only the Red Forman’s and Stan Smiths of the world think your all-things-considered obligation would be to inform the police of his crimes.

III.

Here are some objections people have to the gratitude theory.

Objection #1: When a benefactor is morally obligated to confer a benefit, duties of gratitude don’t arise; but the government is morally obligated to keep us safe, provide healthcare, etc., so we have no debt of gratitude to the government when it does those things.

Reply: I reject the starting premise. If I get hit by a car and you find me lying on the road, you are morally obligated to help me if it’s at minimal cost to yourself; but, if you do help me, I clearly still have a duty of gratitude.

Objection #2: The government, as a whole, makes no special sacrifice—or if it does, very little—when it benefits you in particular; but you only owe a debt of gratitude when your benefactor made some serious, special sacrifice in an effort to benefit your.

Reply: I deny that you don’t owe a debt of gratitude when no serious, special sacrifice was made to benefit you in particular. If you found me drowning and all you had to do was toss a small rubber ring like it was the easiest thing in the world, I think I still incur an obligation of gratitude.

Objection #3: You only have a duty of gratitude if you’re (meaningfully) able to reject the benefits you receive. But it’s extremely hard to avoid receiving any benefits from your government. To avoid the security it provides, you might need to flee your country for a War Zone, or the South Pole. So, you have no debt of gratitude to the government.

Reply #3: You can incur duties of gratitude for benefits that you could not have rejected—in fact, such duties are extremely widespread. If someone carries you in their womb for nine months, for example, you do have an obligation of gratitude to that person, even though, because you were so little, you had very little say in the matter.

Objection #4: Sometimes the government majorly screws over its citizens—e.g., confines them to life in a slum, subjects them to apartheid, imprisons them unjustly, etc. So, the gratitude theory is the only theory we employ, won’t that mean that some people don’t have a duty to obey the law in cases where it harms no one, when they won’t get caught, etc.

Reply #4: Yes, and this is the right result. If the government fails to keep you safe, routinely disrespects you, spits in your face, steals your house, shoots your dog, etc., and then tells you not to smoke a menthol cigarette in the privacy of your own home where the only victim of your behaviour is you, it’s not intuitive—to me, at least—that you have any non-self-protective reason to obey that law. The duty to obey is something that states must earn—they don’t just get it for free.

Objection #5: Even if we owe a duty of gratitude to the state, duties of gratitude can be fulfilled in all kinds of ways, by conferring all kinds of benefits on one’s benefactor. One way to pay back the state might be to do what they tell me (within reason), but another way might be to, e.g., write influential blog posts against philosophical anarchist, spreading awareness about all the good things the government does for us, etc.5

Reply: Suppose you bake me a scrumptious vegan cake when I’m poorly that totally makes my week, and I incur a duty of gratitude. At that stage, I could discharge my debt of gratitude in multiple different ways: by writing a thank you note, making you vegan cupcakes, etc.

But suppose I’m the considerate type, and I ask you, “What can I do for you?” You are British about it at first and say “no no, I don’t want anything”, but I insist, and eventually you crack and ask me to share some of my vegan biscuits that I have lying next to me. Once you say that, my duty to benefit in some generic way hardens into a duty to benefit you in this, very precise way.

Suppose, now, I don’t ask out loud what I can do for you, but I know ahead of time that if I asked that question, you would 100% ask for some of my biscuits. In that case, I think, I have a perfect duty to benefit you precisely my sharing by biscuits, not in some other way.

In the case of the government, I am nearly certain that if I sent a letter to my head of state, or asked a question of parliament, or whatever, whether they would rather I obey all their laws or disobey some of their laws (in particular, the laws that it wouldn’t be independently immoral to violate, like those against jaywalking) but benefit them in some other way, like writing really influential blog posts that help to rekindle faith in government, the official position of the government, qua group, would be that they want me to obey the law.

(This is true, I claim, even if each politician would privately prefer that I break the law and write my influential, pro-government blog posts; as I’ll argue in the next reply, the political obligation of gratitude is owed to the government, not the individuals who make it up. Consequently, it’s what the government wants, qua collective body, that matters, not what individual political actors want. And group desires are not reducible to the aggregate desires of group members.)

Objection #6: Duties of gratitude only arise when your benefactor benefits you intentionally. But governments are groups, and groups can’t literally ‘intend’ things.6

Reply #6: I agree that duties of gratitude only arise when benefits are conferred intentionally; to take an example from Simmons, suppose you’re being mugged, but I inadvertently save you by walking by, scaring off the mugger with my big, hulking frame. In that case, even if you’re grateful that I walked by, you don’t incur a duty of gratitude.

What I disagree with (at least in my persona as devil’s advocate), is the implausible, unmotivated, reductionist view that groups don’t literally have motives and intentions that are irreducible to the motives and intentions of individuals.

There is a ginormous and very boring academic literature on collective intentionally and anti-reductionist approaches thereto. To spare you some of that, here is one-paragraph statement of the case from Timothy Williamson:

“[A]scriptions of intentional action or intention to a collective subject are arguably irreducible to ascriptions of intentional action or intention to its members. When the selection committee intends to offer the job to a given candidate, nothing much follows about the intentions of its members, who may negligently fail to form any appropriate intentions, or treacherously form intentions to subvert the committee’s decision.”

The committee example is a good one. Suppose a selection committee unanimously votes to hire you, starting Friday; in that case, it seems true that the committee intends to hire you, starting Friday.

But suppose, privately, each individual committee member belonged to a different Millenarian sect, such that they all believed, with alarming certainty, that Christ would return on Thursday and rapture us all into Heaven. As a result, no individual member of the board intends, with the others, to hire you on Friday; even still, the committee intends to hire you on Friday.

Applied to the government: even in cases where every politician is a devious so-and-so who is only in it for himself, the government can—qua group—literally intend to benefit you, in a manner that is irreducible to the intentions of the politicians and civil servants who comprise it.

(A related objection might be that groups—like governments—do no literally have benevolent motives. I find it hard to respond to this objection in a concise way because there is no general agreement on what a ‘motive’ is; but presumably, it has something to do with a agent’s desires, beliefs, and intentions. I won’t go into it here, but there are similar anti-reductionist arguments for irreducible group desires (“What do we want? Climate justice!”) and irreducible group beliefs, in addition to irreducible group intentions. So whatever a ‘motive’ is, the defender of this objection has their work cut out for them if they want to lean on this objection.

IV.

As it happens, I think there are at least two pretty decent objections to the gratitude theory, and for that reason I’m reluctant to accept it. Unfortunately, I will have to leave in in suspense, because it is time to vacate the library.

My parting message is just that the gratitude theory of political obligation is underrated; the reasons it’s normally rejected on the basis of are lame, and we should all be more grateful that its here.

It would be peculiar to deny political legitimacy but affirm political obligation, but it’s technically a possible view; for example, you could think the government has standing to demand that people do things, but no standing to threaten them with force if they don’t do those things. E.g., I might have standing to demand you to apologise, giving you a duty to apologise, but lack the standing to threaten you with violence if you refuse to do so. (You might ask, but isn’t ‘government’ by definition the monopoly on coercion within a given geographical area? Perhaps, but in theory you could have a government

2

3

Quoted in: Simmons, A. John. (1979). Moral Principles and Political Obligations. Princeton: Princeton University Press: p. 161.

4
